#6186. Rail To The Austin Airport Is Back On The Table—After Costs Soared And A Voter Bait-and-Switch

Austin’s airport used to be super convenient but it’s outgrown itself. There are just too many passengers for the size of the facility, at peak times it can be nearly body to body as you navigate through the terminal. What was once curb-to-gate in minutes, security wait times on peak travel days can be quite long. And traffic gets backed up heading into and out of the airport. There’s a long trek across the road and through a parking garage, up and down levels, to get to Uber or taxis. They’re building a new terminal and a new headhouse. The airport’s solution is to get (a lot) bigger. It will never recapture the ease of a smaller airport, and it’s going to mean more walking and showing up even earlier. One thing Austin doesn’t have is rail to the airport. Voters approved higher property taxes in 2020 to pay for it, but the cost of the project ballooned and train ambitions remained – but the airport connection got axed to save money. Now the mayor wants to start the process of planning again for a train to the airport. The much smaller light rail system now being developed will cost nearly double what was once estimated, even though it won’t reach the airport when it’s supposed to open in 2033. But since the airport is building an entirely new face to the facility, it makes sense to plan for how a train would approach and where the station would go. Plus, they’re going to be looking to have the airport pay for a portion of it. That’s part of what the mayor means when he talks about rail reaching the airport without new tax money. Mayor Kirk Watson lays out a three-mile extension of the planned train, mostly elevated, with a station at the airport. He says the Federal Transit Administration has agreed to a streamlined environmental review, and the next nine to twelve months will be spent working through costs and funding. His challenge is to deliver it “within our existing budget approved by voters – no new taxpayer dollars.” Latest #WatsonWire: It’s time to start the process to get rail to the airport. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past. We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it. The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come. As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city. A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel. We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA. An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact. Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1. In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps. We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed. With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport. Read more: https://t.co/JTYqnnRyEE — Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026 Airport Rail Was Part Of What Voters Were Sold Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past.

We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it.

The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come.

As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city.

A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel.

We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA.

An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact.

Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1.

In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps.

We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed.

With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport.

— Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026

Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However,

And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share.

Back in 2016 when I first started traveling to Austin frequently, the airport was one of the easier destinations to get in and out of. Then they moved Uber and Lyft to the remote parking lot 4 city blocks from the terminal doors and causing you to have drag your baggage upstairs, or downstairs to get to the pickup area depending on what level you exited the terminal. Not very convenient at all, and now, it has become very congested at times and all of the eating establishments and concessions are basically overrun at lunch, dinner, and breakfast. I hope they do the rebuild right.

The fundamental problem with light-rail systems is simple: How do people get from their homes to a rail stop?

If they have to drive (and park) there, they may as well just drive the rest of the way to their destination.

“ Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for.”

It’s quite common that driving & parking at a rail station then taking the train is far faster & cheaper than driving & parking at a major destination (such as an airport).

Voters never learn that transit systems always cost several times the original estimates while delivering less than promised. Austin’s results are nevertheless better than LAX’s people mover, let alone California’s high speed rail money pit. I thought that Oakland wasted $800 million on a BART connector to replace shuttle buses, but later projects are almost making that look like a bargain.

Too many make the mistake of believing the progressives when they say they want rail service to anywhere. They don’t really care if a single foot of track is ever laid down or not They only purpose of the rail projects is to siphon billions of dollars from taxpayers to well connected progressive companies and NGO’s. True in CA and LAX, and will be the same in Austin.

As they say history repeats itself. When SeaTac made it’s first renovation, it was more important to build parking garage adjacent to terminal then a light rail station. When light rail finally started is was projected so far over budget that federales were going pull funding. The City went back to taxpayers who swallowed and said ok. So, you can now take the light rail downtown to the airport painlessly(until you pay taxes on it).

Now, you can get on as far north as Lynwood(Everett planned). Also, you can go from UW to airport. And within the past year, you can go to and from Bellevue and Redmond(Microsoft hq). And that is a first by light rail over the Lake Washington floating bridge. A world’s first. So Gary, it only costs an unbelievable amount of taxpayer money.

For the majority of people with the means to avoid light rail, they will do so, just like they avoid buses for the same reason. Just ask Iryna Zarutska.

RE: TexasTJ. LOL. I remember doing miles runs for early flights at JFK. When I got on the A train at around 4 AM, it was like a homeless hotel. I was like the only non-homeless on the train. Also, I never actually missed a flight due to train stoppages. But I was always afraid I would.

#6185. The Nvidia Scandal Is a Warning Shot

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to the media on the day he attends a meeting between Chinese Premier Li Qiang and U.S. business representatives at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, May 14, 2026.

Many Americans have their doubts about our cutting-edge AI, but as the drama now surrounding Nvidia seems to suggest, the Beijing regime does not feel the same way.

As a reminder, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, put out a statement in which he admitted to having had an extramarital affair. The “other woman” has been identified in numerous reports as Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national.

Ms. Huang joined Megaspeed, a Singaporean company at around the time it moved into the data-center business shortly after a Biden-era tightening of export controls on advanced chips. She was briefly its managing director and sole shareholder and is believed to retain an executive role. She has not commented publicly on Mr. Huang’s admission. Her current whereabouts are unknown.

The principal focus of Megaspeed’s operations has been described as renting out computing power relying on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities) to its customers, enabling them to use it remotely. This is allowed, with exceptions, under U.S. law. What is not permitted is for the most advanced chips of this type to be exported to China. Little is known about Megaspeed’s client base (other than that it included Alibaba, the Chinese technology and e-commerce group), ultimate ownership (Ms. Huang had meanwhile sold her interest), or funding.

Megaspeed and, reportedly, Ms. Huang have attracted the attention of the U.S. authorities. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling contraband chips to China. U.S. intelligence is said to have been aware of Ms. Huang’s relationship with Nvidia’s CEO and identified her as a Chinese spy, information reportedly passed on to senior officials in Washington. Megaspeed has denied the allegations against it (investigation of which was abruptly transferred from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department). Up until now, Nvidia has said that it found nothing amiss. China has rejected allegations of any spy plot.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation. Mr. Huang has said he will cooperate. The FBI is also digging, and Congress is taking a closer look. The investigations will reveal what they will reveal. Mr. Huang’s obligations as a husband are a matter solely for him and his family. As a CEO, however, it looks as if, to put it mildly, he has taken risks that he should not have. Unless he made some preemptive disclosures, the affair posed obvious intertwined questions about conflict of interest (Megaspeed was a large client after all), national security, and the threat of blackmail, all issues of which he must have been aware. Even if he has broken no laws, he appears to have put Nvidia into a position in which it should not have been. This story, as we know it so far, also raises issues about Nvidia’s corporate governance (who, if anyone, was keeping an eye on Huang?) and its relationship with the government. Who knew what and when, and what did they do, if anything, about it?

Handling this will be complicated by the nature of the AI “arms race” with China. It is a competition in which the U.S. is primarily participating through its private, not public, sector. To be sure, private companies were heavily involved in the Cold War’s arms and space races but mainly as government contractors, a relationship in which Washington, as the customer, set the agenda — and the rules. This time around, the private sector is leading the way, driven by its ambition to compete commercially. It is ahead of China to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. China wants to win the AI race. So must we, and we must act accordingly.

That will require recognizing how critical Nvidia currently is. It supplies about 90 percent of the microchips used for training AI and 70 percent of those needed to run LLMs, and it is using its cash to play an important part in funding the development of America’s AI ecosystem. Its role will become less dominant — free markets and changing market leadership go hand in hand — but for the government to apply a wrecking ball to the company now would be madness.

There clearly need to be changes to the way that Nvidia, which is unusually dependent on one man, Jensen Huang, is run, and there needs to be accountability for what has taken place. But assuming his missteps turn out to be a matter of a terrible lapse and nothing more, the changes needed will probably be evolutionary rather than revolutionary. We should not want the disappearance of the executive energy that has made Nvidia the colossus it has become.

We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Mr. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

Finally, it must be hoped that politicians do not exploit the fresh indignation now being stirred up about an already unpopular industry for their own purposes. To do so risks hobbling American AI. And that would hand Beijing a win far greater than anything that Megaspeed or Ms. Huang might have delivered.

#6184. Hyatt Hotel Promises Jonathan Adler Toiletries—But There’s Drugstore Shampoo On Its Housekeeping Cart

Hotel Avante in Mountain View, California advertises Jonathan Adler bath amenities. A reader photographed its housekeeping cart with a retail bottle of HASK shampoo resting among unbranded squeeze bottles. This is another JdV by Hyatt property, just a few miles from the Wild Palms hotel where I reported on DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. Apparently readers need to keep checking what’s on the carts. The brown bottle is HASK Tea Tree Oil & Rosemary Invigorating Shampoo, in the 12-ounce size. HASK is an affordable retail hair care brand, with products sold at CVS and other stores. Around it are condiment-style squeeze bottles. At least one has “Body wash” handwritten on tape. That identifies the type of product, without telling guests whose product it is. It seems like Hyatt a good reason to check what this hotel is using to refill its toiletries. But they had this reason at its sister property, too. There needs to be much stronger monitoring. Hyatt’s Hotel Avante page lists “Jonathan Adler bath amenities” across all six room categories. The hotel’s separate website promises that as well. I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand. The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care. Then in January, Ben at One Mile at a Time published follow-up photos showing the bulk jugs with their labels removed. Wild Palms still advertises Jonathan Adler toiletries. I just wrote about the ketchup, mustard and mayonnaise bottle approach to hotel toiletries. Once the hotel keeps reusing the branded packaging, it can change the contents without changing anything the guest sees. An owner who substitutes a cheaper product keeps the savings, while Hyatt and the advertised toiletry company risk their reputations. Remind me again why bulk dispensers were a better idea than single use biodegradable packaging? I understand the dismay of false advertising but does anyone really pick a hotel based on the shampoo or soap offered vs loyalty points, location, free/discounted parking and breakfast, and location? I’m seriously interested.

@Ray: Pretty much any legitimate brand of shampoo would be acceptable to me, but I still don’t find it acceptable to advertise one brand and refill the bottles with a different brand.

If the shampoo bottles in the shower were labeled Suave, and we saw bulk bottles of Suave on the housekeepers’ carts (in the original packaging from Unilever, not bottles with handwritten labels on tape), that would give me more confidence with regard to the hotel’s shampoo policy than what this Hyatt is doing.

It wasn’t. I have some sympathy for the environmental argument for the re-usable bottles, but corporate culture in the US showing [again] that they will take advantage of anything they can to save a buck. The bulk bottles on the wall were never a good idea, if for no other reason than hygene (who thinks they replace these once a year, if at all). But this is another reason. Taking advantage of customers, even at ‘luxury’ properties. Makes me wonder if we overvalue hotels and should just go straight to Fairfield Inn.

And these are just the instances we know about. If there are confirmed sightings of this in the past couple of months, imagine the actual scope of the problem, I assume this is going on at thousands of hotels.

If I were at Jonathan Adler, I’d start off by suing Hyatt for false marketing (or legal equivalent). For us guests, seems like it’s time to start pushing legislation that will force compliance. Require unopened, personal-size bottles of toiletries in every room. I have no problem with requiring it to be biodegradable, but even without this, seems reasonable from a hygiene standpoint. Even anllowing accurately labeled [bulk] bottles might be a slippery slope – if hotels have openly flouted that by using ‘ketchup’ bottles to refill, I imagine their reaction to comply might be to buy a single bulk bottle of advertised brand for each cart, then keep refilling that with the cheap sub.

On the other hand, maybe hotels would just revolt and stop providing these toiletries as amenities. As a traveller, might be a PITA to bring my own, but preferable to what seems to be going on now.

It all comes out of the same large industrial drum in the basement labeled “Universal Cleaner Base – 200 L – Made in China.”

@Emcampbe and others: It was NEVER about the environment. Never. It was ALWAYS about thinking of a way they could market sh*t and get people to accept it — even praise them for it.

We’ve seen that very thing in comments on in these forums: Person A complains about this sort of con-job, and Person B comes back with, “Hey, at least they’re trying to save the planet.”

I fully agree with @Emcampbe that the first step should be for Adler to sue them, arguing Hyatt is knowingly damaging their brand by passing off inferior products as theirs. If the neighborhood Piggly Wiggly starting putting name brand labels on cheap generics it would be an easy lawsuit. This is no different.

Why would a libertarian law professor have a toiletry brand?

One real issue here is that I have allergies to some brands and if they were substituted in and I didn’t know, my skin might break out.

I agree that the switch isn’t a good look. I just feel like is no benefit in advertising a brand. Just list shampoo supplied.

Of the chains, Hyatt properties are the most egregious offenders of using condiment-style bottles to squeeze unknown products into dispensers that are never cleaned or sanitized. I’ve even seen this at Grand Hyatt properties.

I think it’s high time the elites are forced to use these low-quality products.

I’m not a shampoo snob, I don’t have enough hair to be one but this can cause some real problems for people with alleges.

Some are allergic/ sensitive to tea tree oil. I bring my own products because I don’t want to worry about a reaction away from home. Most will never have an issue.

@Ray Not the shampoo itself, but if a hotel quietly swaps what it advertises I’d wonder what else on the listing is loose. For the stuff you mention I compare the full stay, room plus parking and breakfast, not the headline rate. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from a bunch of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory differ by country. Then let location decide

@Matt — You know what would solve this… better consumer protections… *wink*

@Maryland — Tried to mention to you earlier this week, I finally made it to western PA. Thank you again for recommending.

1990 great. Snow moving in any time. So many acres. So sad. I cry thinking about it

No one who travels likes the large bottles in the shower. Who knows what people put into them. I travel with my own soap etc. I don’t want any surprises.

@RT – I’ve known Jonathan for 30 years, and he never mentioned it to me! 😉

There are real working solutions already employed by other industries for this problem that keep operators honest while still allowing multi use containers. Welcome to the stage Heinz ketchup.

That company that figured it all out and have pretty successfully stopped every trick in the book by restaurants trying to get away with refilling Heinz bottles with cheaper crappier products.

They do things like: – Sell large multi use bottles to restaurants but do not allowing refilling in their contracts, they must be replaced. – they have created dispenser systems that can only be refilled by replacing internal sealed bags that cant be refilled (those big Heinz branded condiment boxes you use the pump handle to get ketchup out of). – They give restaurants Heinz bottles that are always transparent and the label has a red outline around the ages that is perfectly color matched with Heinz ketchup so is largely invisible when filled with Heinz ketchup but sticks out clearly when the bottle is full of a different brand’s ketchup. – And most of all they aggressively audit restaurants and sue if they find violations. – Probably way more tricks of the trade then that too.

The toiletry brands should employ some of the same techniques with hotels, they are not that hard. As long as the hotel is not lying about it and keeping them sanitized I actually like the user experience of larger multi use products as I like liquid soap better then bars and you don’t run out if your sharing a room with another person.

@Maryland — It was so well-done. Lost it at the ‘tower of voices’… windy day; it was like they were singing. And how they included the child for Ms. Grancolas. The answering machines. Wow. (Winter isn’t all bad; would like to return, someday, maybe see Fallingwater in the snow.) Take care out there.

Love it. Hard core political discussions (vs. travel discussions) to shampoo snobbery.. A real eclectic site.

I was at the tower of voices before the actual opening. The place is spiritual. And falling water. Is part of my history. Try the Nemacolin resort nearby for an awesome array of summer activity. Who doesn’t want to drive hummers over rocks and shoot guns? Maggie also has another less expensive hotel nearby . They filmed that bachelor series there if you are looking for a date….always. Maryland

Saw a car with Maryland plates and a cute bumper sticker with “tell your dog I said hi” (Thought of you! Unlike Matthew, I love dogs…Bah!)

@Quinn…agreeed. If I was a brand promoted on the bottle and my product wasn’t in there, I’d sue them for sure. As someone mentioned, some people have allergies to specific ingredients. Not that the ingredients are necessarily on the labels in hotels, but those people probably have a good idea what brands to steer clear of. Would be great for someone to have a reaction, sue the product manufacturer and then find out it wasn’t their product.

All about the chip, chip, chip to keep increasing profits.

#6182. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

#6181. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

Story is full of holes and relies on many chain of coincidence. But then again, people these days are getting dumber.

Genter is, more than anything else, a content creator. Content is not created under oath. Believe it was stolen, believe his fellow content creator was genuinely in DC, watching bus stops, but maybe a grain of salt on the "medicines and priceless memories" or whatever. A bottle of Gaviscon? It makes a good story, which is why we all clicked and are still with it, deep in the comments. these guys aren't wrong.

Many will recognize JT Genter as a seasoned traveler. His medicines were in a checked bag and not carry-on? Unwise.

irreplaceable items in your checked luggage...? Really? medication in your checked luggage...? Really? i call bs on this.

I rarely check bags but if I do once I get off the flight I'm immediately down at the baggage claim for this very reason. And I stand near where the bags are coming out so there's no chance of anyone walking off with my bag. It might not be right but in today's arrest and immediately release back out on the streets to do it again environment you need to take precautions. This thief might even be required to take a class as his punishment.

#6180. The Two Card Answer To Which Rewards Strategy Is Actually Best

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

When I talk to people about earning miles, it’s inescapable that the majority of miles are earned from rewards credit cards. Most people want to know simply, “what is the best credit card.” If pressed I do have an answer to that question, but the best answer is that it’s usually two different credit cards that you pair together, taking the best of each.

The first thing to understand about rewards cards is that, in addition to their basic features as a payments tool, bundled financing, and consumer protections, there are really three different ways a card adds value. You need to understand this to make sure you’re using yours in the right way.

Initial bonus. A card might offer 100,000 points as an acquisition bonus. That’s a great reason to get a card, but it isn’t a good reason to keep the card or to spend money on the card (once you’ve earned the bonus).

Benefits. You might get free checked bags or priority boarding, lounge access, for free Disney+. Those can be great reasons to have the card, and keep the card, but aren’t reasons to spend money on the card (outside of the spend on those activities, potentially).

Rebate on spend. The most rewarding card for the kind of spending you’re doing – that means earning the most points, and the most valuable points, that you can redeem for the rewards you value most. When people ask about the best card, they’re usually talking about the one that gives them the best return on their spending. Although if they value a card’s benefits, they need to be careful to keep that issue separate – get that card, sure, enjoy the benefits, but don’t just default to using it for spending, too. I think that the American Express Platinum Card® (see rates and fees) is great to have, it is incredibly valuable for its benefits, but my goodness do not actually spend money on that card outside of airline tickets. For spending the reason you want two cards is that you generally want (1) that earns the most points in the categories you spend the most, and (2) a card that earns more than one point per dollar on everything else. Don’t fall into the trap of getting a ‘grocery card’ and then earning just one point per dollar on everything else. You can frequently get two cards where the second one has no annual fee, even. Here are some of the very best pairings: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (See rates and fees) has an offer to earn 100k bonus points after you spend $8,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. What’s great is earning 3x (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases) on travel, shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, advertising purchases made with social media sites and search engines each account anniversary year. It has the same points transfer partners as Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees). And if you have some of the no annaul fee Chase cards, you can move the points from those cards over to Ink Business Preferred and then transfer them to airlines and hotel programs. And there are a number of Chase cards with no annual fee that earn points quickly, but on their own those points can’t be transferred to airlines or hotels. But if you earn points with one of those, you can transfer the points to your Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card and from there to miles and points in other programs. For instance, the Ink Business Cash card earns 5x on the first $25,000 in combined purchases at office stores and on internet, cable and phone services each account anniversary year. It earns 2x on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases at gas stations and restaurants each account anniversary year. Freedom Flex earns 3X on dining and at drugstores and 5x in rotating categories, on up to $1,500 spend each quarter. The Freedom Unlimited card earns 1.5x on all spend (but 3x on dining and at drugstores). I have multiple Freedom and Ink Business cards, personally. Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) has a $95 annual fee. It earns 3x on groceries, dining, gas stations and on EV charging as well as flights and hotels. That’s really strong. It’s offering 60,000 bonus ThankYou® Points after spending $4,000 in the first 3 months of account opening. And the points even transfer to American Airlines AAdvantage miles. oneworld: American Airlines AAdvantage, Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Qatar Airways Privilege Club Star Alliance: Avianca LifeMiles, EVA Air Infinity MileageLands, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Thai Airways Royal Orchid Plus, Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles SkyTeam: Air France KLM Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Non-alliance: Emirates Skywards, Etihad Guest, JetBlue TrueBlue Hotels: Leading Hotels of the World Leaders Club, Accor ALL – Accor Live Limitless, Choice Hotels Choice Privileges, Preferred Hotels I Prefer, Wyndham Hotels Wyndham Rewards There’s also a $100 Annual Hotel Benefit. Once per calendar year, you receive $100 off a single hotel stay of $500 or more (excluding taxes and fees) when booked through CitiTravel.com, applied instantly at time of booking. You can supplement that strong earner with a Citi Double Cash card which earns 2x on everything and has no annual fee. If you were going to get just one card for your spending, set it and forget it, and didn’t want to juggle products then I think the single best heavy spending card has to be the Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees). It’s a $495 annual fee card. It earns the most points on most spending, and it earns the most valuable points. The only thing to flag is that there are some things, like tax payments, that it doesn’t earn points for. So if you’re relying on big quarterly tax deposits for your points-earning this isn’t the card for you. You can earn 50,000 Bilt Points after spending $4,000 on everyday purchases in the first 90 days + $300 of Bilt Cash. The card earns 2X points on everyday spend. Plus, you can use Bilt Cash to earn 3x on up to $25,000 in purchases, you get a $200 twice annual hotel credit (with a 2-night minimum stay), and earning the card’s 50,000 point bonus after $4,000 in non-housing spend in the first 3 months also gives you Gold status for a year and that lets you earn Bilt points through Rakutent at 1:1. You can earn 3.3 points per dollar when spending 75% of the amount of your rent or mortgage and then using Bilt Cash to earn points when paying through through Bilt, and then earn 3 points per dollar redeeming Bilt Cash for points accelerator. So the cap on earning 3 points or more is much higher than that. There’s actually a strategy to earn 4 points per dollar on all of your spending by foregoing Bilt Cash entirely. You can spend points at 1.25 cents apiece directly through their travel portal, and they have the best transfer partners (and biggest transfer bonuses). #6179. The Logic-less Crusade That Just Killed a Data Center

Do activists believe that the $5 billion that would have been spent on this project is just waiting to be allocated elsewhere?

An aerial view of a 49.5-megawatt, three-level data center under construction in Vernon, Calif., April 14, 2026. Inset: Taylor Frazier McCollum

Mario Tama/Getty Images, Screenshot via Electric Llama/YouTube

Meet Taylor Frazier McCollum. McCollum just led a successful movement to block the construction of a $5 billion data center campus in Prince George’s County, Md. Simultaneously, McCollum is upset that her county’s government will not pay for a new roof for her grandfather’s home. Somehow, McCollum cannot see the connection between these two things. In an interview with NPR, she explained that the data center project prompted her political “awakening” and boasted that “so many people are depending on this fight to be successful.”

Are they? Prince George’s County is not in good shape. It has a budget deficit of more than $130 million. Unemployment is high. Last year, the Six Flags amusement park there closed permanently, and in the next few years, the Washington Commanders NFL team intends to move out. The FBI is also trying to leave. McCollum’s father believes that his daughter is a hero in the mold of Medgar Evers, who was killed trying to integrate Mississippi’s schools, or of Martin Luther King. “People like Taylor,” he says, “jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress.”

#6177. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights Again: Will They Resume In December?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. Is that actually happening now, or what exactly is going on?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Interestingly, the airline has promised to provide a schedule update by November 12, 2026, but that date has now come and gone, and there was no update.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of December, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. The company does have a section on its travel updates page with FAQs, and one of the questions is “will the dates change again?” The answer is “we chose dates we are confident in,” but also notes that “if anything changes, you will hear from us first.”

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in December.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. That timeline has come and gone, and now the airline claims it’ll resume operations as of December 2026. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6176. American Kept Charging A $75 Award Fee After No More Work Was Was Required, Former Loyalty Chief Says

American Airlines used to charge $75 to book an award ticket within 21 days of departure. Now the former head of AAdvantage says the airline kept collecting its expedite fee even after the process it was supposed to expedite became automated. Maya Leibman, who ran AAdvantage before becoming American’s Chief Information Officer, discussed this on the this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. The airline finally eliminated the fee in January 2020. Leibman was defending checked bag fees because there are people and equipment involved in moving bags. Then she offered an example of a fee she couldn’t defend. I think she’s wrong about bag fees based on cost of production (‘real cost fallacy’). Bags are charged as a form of price discrimination. Nonetheless, Leibman recalled the transition from a manual award process to online booking: “we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days.”

Maya Leibman, who ran AAdvantage before becoming American’s Chief Information Officer, discussed this on the this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. The airline finally eliminated the fee in January 2020.

Leibman was defending checked bag fees because there are people and equipment involved in moving bags. Then she offered an example of a fee she couldn’t defend. I think she’s wrong about bag fees based on cost of production (‘real cost fallacy’). Bags are charged as a form of price discrimination. Nonetheless, Leibman recalled the transition from a manual award process to online booking:

“we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days.”

The transaction, she pointed out, was “all done automatically.” The fee survived even though the narrative used to justify it was gone. The $75 close-in charge was waived for American’s elite frequent flyers.

American once tried to go further. In May 2008 they announced a $5 charge for booking award tickets on their website. The argument for telephone booking fees had been that agents cost money, and customers could avoid that charge by doing the work themselves online. Here American wanted to charge for the cheaper booking channel, too. I wrote about the announcement on May 30, 2008. Multiply millions of award redemptions by $5 and it was clearly a revenue opportunity since they were the monopoly redeemer of the currency. Members couldn’t take their AAdvantage miles and book travel somewhere else. Except the airline had already used the prospect of an award to persuade customers to earn those miles. Adding a charge when they tried to use them reduced the value of a reward they’d earned, and made it less likely they’d earn in the future. It left a bad taste in the customer’s mouth at exactly the moment they’re supposed to feel best about giving the airline business. As I wrote years ago, American never implemented that fee. They backed away without announcing the reversal. They took the criticism for imposing it and didn’t claim credit for listening to members. The Airline Had Already Been Paid To Give You Those Miles I don’t think airline prices have to track the cost of each transaction. Two passengers on the same flight, in the same cabin, pay different fares every day. Airlines price based on demand. There’s even an economic argument for charging more for last-minute awards: the airline might otherwise sell that seat for an expensive ticket, or the customer might otherwise pay cash for that expensive ticket. In the former case, revenue management is supposed to price the award so that’s not an issue. And neither case requires someone to hurry up and process an electronic ticket. Ultimately, eliminating a cash fee doesn’t even necessarily mean make awards cheaper. When American dropped its $75 charge, I pointed out that United and Delta had moved towards collecting more miles for close-in awards instead. That’s a bad trade for elites who used to have the cash fee waived but don’t get the extra mileage requirement waived. American stopped discounting awards to elites. #6175. Chase Sapphire Reserve Business Bonus: 200K Points Welcome Offer

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business bonus currently offers up to 200,000 Ultimate Rewards points, which is in line with the highest ever publicly available welcome offers that we’ve seen on the card.

While the Sapphire Reserve Business has a steep annual fee, it also offers strong perks, so I’m sure many people will have no issues justifying this annual fee. Either way, if you’re eligible for the card and can complete the spending requirement, this welcome offer is incredibly tempting, and a great reason to apply for the card.

#6174. Why Policy Will Make a Comeback in 2028

Within both major parties, dramatic ideological battles will play out in the presidential race.

With the midterms now behind us, the political world has already shifted to speculation about the next presidential race. While I am not quite ready to make any horse race bets, I will venture to make an even bolder prediction: 2028 will be the election when policy makes a comeback.

At risk of being accused of romanticizing the past, I will freely acknowledge that there was never any golden age in which presidential campaigns were focused on sober-minded discussions about the finer points of policy. Go back through the decades, and in every election, you will find complaints about how elections were much more focused on personalities and trivial matters than serious issues.

Darren Hulst, Vice President, Commercial Marketing, Boeing

Moderated by Seth Borko, Head of Research, Skift

Aviation’s next phase of growth will require airlines, manufacturers, and airports to make long-term investment decisions around sharply different regional demand patterns. Boeing’s Darren Hulst forecasts a doubling of annual global passenger traffic over the next 20 years, while identifying production capacity, supplier readiness and fleet replacement needs as major factors in the industry’s ability to accommodate that expansion.

#6170. Ken Paxton Spotted Fleeing Texas With Girlfriend After Voters Reject His Senate Bid—Flying Coach To Fiji

Eight days after losing his U.S. Senate race, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was photographed at San Francisco airport with his girlfriend, Tracy Duhon, wearing a straw hat and carrying a Republican Attorneys General Association backpack. They were apparently headed to Fiji. And photos show them in coach. They departed Wednesday night, November 11. A witness says they worried about their bags making it to Fiji. Michael Board shares the photo of Ken Paxton and Tracy Duhon at San Francisco airport Another photo shows them standing in the aisle of coach. TMZ: Ken Paxton spotted in San Francisco International Airport, witness says he was traveling to Fiji https://t.co/GNFXuDuPvY — Kalshi Politics (@KalshiPolitics) November 12, 2026 Meanwhile, Paxton’s divorce finalized Thursday. State Senator Angela Paxton filed to end their 38-year marriage last year “on biblical grounds.” I’ve covered the travels of Ted Cruz, Elizabeth Warren, AOC, Bernie Sanders and others, and the credit card spend habits of former Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker. This choice isn’t partisan. Paxton Has A History Of Getting Out Of Town A Texas politician fleeing the state for warmer climes brings to mind Ted Cruz flying to Cancún during the February 2021 winter storm while millions of Texans were without power. This time the disaster was electoral. But Paxton has his own winter storm escape story. He and his then-wife went to Utah during that same freeze, saying he had meetings with Utah’s attorney general about the state Google antitrust case. This summer, I wrote about Paxton spending America’s 250th birthday in London with Duhon. He marked the anniversary of separating from Britain by going to Britain. The pair had been spotted traveling through Washington Dulles on their way to Iceland in late June. Then came the London video, with Marriott County Hall in the background. They apparently flew economy on that trip. Video of Ken Paxton and Tracy Duhon in London over the Fourth of July weekend In October, the Wall Street Journal reported on video of Paxton and Duhon celebrating New Year’s Eve 2024 overlooking the Burj Khalifa fireworks with fugitives indicted in a federal healthcare fraud case who had contributed $190,000 to Paxton’s campaign. James Talarico’s campaign shares footage of Ken Paxton at the Dubai gathering Republicans Knew Who They Were Nominating The Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Attorney General Paxton. Paxton’s own senior staff reported him to the FBI. House investigators alleged that an Austin real estate developer provided home renovations and helped conceal Paxton’s activities, including through an Uber account under the name “Dave P.” He also employed a woman Paxton previously had an affair with. The Uber account apparently let Paxton carry on his affair and visit his donor without his security detail or using his identifiable state vehicle. In return, Paxton allegedly used his office to help the developer. One example was a rushed legal opinion invoking pandemic restrictions to stop foreclosure auctions. The Texas Senate, under pressure large donors and the Lieutenant Governor, acquitted him in 2023. He’d also spent years under state felony securities fraud charges. That case ended through an agreement requiring restitution, community service and ethics training. The federal corruption investigation ended without charges. President Trump endorsed Paxton against incumbent Senator John Cornyn a week before their May runoff. Republicans then had to spend heavily defending a seat they’d held for decades, with a candidate that may have been one of the worst campaigners I’ve seen in 30 years even apart from his past challenges. Here he is wearing a reported-$40,000 watch and a Four Seasons golf shirt. And this clip of him was promoted by his campaign: .@KenPaxtonTX: The future of our state and the future of our country ride on this race. https://t.co/2ZvVWdhwzp — Paxton War Room (@PaxtonsPatriots) August 29, 2026 That choice cost Republicans dearly. Cornyn would’ve been far better-positioned in the general election. Counterfactuals are hard, but the rest of his party’s nominees at the state level were clearly brought down by his place on the ticket. Republicans even appeared in advertising against him. Former Republican state Representative Glenn Rogers, who’d voted to impeach Paxton, appeared in a pro-Talarico ad saying he’d never trust or support Paxton. The most revealing ad may have been the one Angela Paxton made because polls showed over 10% of Republicans staying home. While divorcing him, she urged Republicans to vote without mentioning her husband by name: “It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line.” Paxton wasn’t the only Republican with problems. Governor Greg Abbott had helped defeat Republican legislators who opposed school choice in the 2024 primaries. That left resentment in rural communities where public schools are major employers, and there are fewer private school options where the vouchers could be used. Republicans also faced a terrible national election environment, with an unpopular President and high gas prices. I Even Agree With Him On Some Of His Lawsuits Just this morning, I wrote about Austin’s airport rail plans and the financing arrangement Paxton’s office challenged. The city raised property taxes, then routed the money through a separate corporation to issue the debt, allowing the city to claim that it isn’t borrowing. Economically, property taxes support the bonds, while the city claims its not running afoul on state borrowing rules. The arrangement is probably illegal, but the state’s new attorney general may not be as inclined to continue the litigation. Credit: Gage Skidmore via Wikimedia Commons Even where they might agree with Paxton on an issue, plenty of Texans would’ve been happy for him to leave much earlier, even without a ticket to Fiji. No flights qualify to Fiji, sadly. Maybe someday the US can adopt similar protections, then Ken and his GF would be covered, if, say, there was a crew member high on cocaine, causing the flight to be cancelled by the airline. Just sayin’…

You know Don wants Natalie to one-up Bill/Monica… somehow.

#6169. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.
