#6080. The Economic Impact of Israel’s Election

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Q&A: The Economic Impact of Israel’s Election

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

Israel has been in political gridlock ever since its elections on Oct. 27, with neither bloc of parties having achieved the clear 61-seat threshold for a majority in parliament. But it’s become evident that financial markets had been hoping for a change of government, with stocks, bonds, and the shekel currency having fallen sharply since the vote. The broader economic implications of the election are also increasingly coming into view.

How have financial markets reacted to the election results? Why has the Israeli economy held up so well during three years of war on multiple fronts? And if Israel suffers further political isolation, how would its economy be impacted?

Israel has been in political gridlock ever since its elections on Oct. 27, with neither bloc of parties having achieved the clear 61-seat threshold for a majority in parliament. But it’s become evident that financial markets had been hoping for a change of government, with stocks, bonds, and the shekel currency having fallen sharply since the vote. The broader economic implications of the election are also increasingly coming into view.

How have financial markets reacted to the election results? Why has the Israeli economy held up so well during three years of war on multiple fronts? And if Israel suffers further political isolation, how would its economy be impacted?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: Going into the election, Israel’s economic baseline in the country seemed pretty strong. The Bank of Israel said it expects the economy to grow by 5 percent next year, and the country still has a low debt-to-GDP ratio. Are there other governments that come to mind as a comparison with this combination of a paralyzed state with such a strong economy underlying it?

Adam Tooze: The obvious parallel is the United States. And I don’t even mean that just simply as sort of a formal comparison, but there is a real connection between the two. The Israeli economy is driven fundamentally by a tech boom at this point. And obviously the links between Israel and the United States are deep, not just at the level of policy and at the levels of subsidy from the U.S., but also culturally between the universities, between the tech ecosystems. The big AI players in the U.S. all have a big presence in Israel and are proud and committed to that. And they are together involved in this war against Iran, which is one of the principal disturbing factors in the world economy, which, if it has a kind of rationale from [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu’s point of view, it’s hard really to see as a sustainable strategy for Israel’s geopolitics going forward and is even more absurd and self-destructive from the American point of views. So in a sense, they’re joined at the hip.

The Israeli economy is really a remarkable story. Its current growth rate is 5.6 percent. The forecast for next year is 7.5 percent. So this is extraordinary growth. Since the Hamas attack on Israel of October 2023, and despite Israel’s then-multiyear project of mass destruction and mass murder, by the October 2026 election, the Tel Aviv stock market gained roughly 130 percent compared to only 80 percent in Wall Street, and the shekel appreciated by 25 percent. So if you had bought Israel on the day of the Hamas attack, you would have made out like gangbusters in the interim. It’s a truly staggering demonstration—as the United States is in its current moment—that there is simply no correlation between capitalist prosperity, growth, speculative gains, technological progress, and any, I think, conventional understanding of political rationality, geopolitics, sustainable politics, conformity to basic standards of law, or, I’m going to say it, human decency. Like, this is a pretty shocking indictment of anyone who comes to the game with a naive assumption that those things go together well. It ain’t true.

So the short answer is, we shouldn’t probably see this as a contradiction. You know, this is what the Germans will say, “ungehemmt,” like unfettered kind of techno-industrial project looks like. Is it sustainable in the long run? Well, almost certainly not. But can it work over the short run? Absolutely, it can. And are we in the United States living in a slightly less excessive version of what’s going on in Israel? In some senses, yes. And our tax dollars, after all, have helped pay for it. And now we’re actually involved in a war side by side with Israel against Iran. So yeah, that’s the obvious analogy.

CA: Obviously there’s been a market reaction to the lack of clarity coming out of this election. And I’m curious to unpack the perspective of financial markets. What was informing those hopes for a change of government? From the perspective of financial markets, what are the relevant considerations here in this election?

AT: Yes, I think there was, generally speaking, a slight favor in the Israeli markets for Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition coalition over Netanyahu’s bloc. And on the day of the election results, the index fell by between 2 and 4 percent. What were the factors driving that preference? Well, there was some hope that an Eisenkot-led government would aim toward geopolitical deescalation. But really how much room is there for that? Maybe on the settler side, there was some hope, because of the different composition of the coalition, that there would be more concessions. But the war with Iran actually has powerful majority backing. And the broader escalation of Israeli hostility toward the Palestinians is now a cliche. I think there’s also deep doubt on the part of financial markets about institutional credibility. And Netanyahu’s utterly ruthless willingness to just put the institutions of the Israeli state and Israeli government through the meat grinder of political opportunism and his own personal political survival is, after all, remarkable.

And what the markets are worried about, as they are in the U.S. as well, is the role of the central bank. The Israeli central bank is a powerful institution and is relatively independent. Netanyahu has shown his willingness to subvert all the other institutions of the Israeli state. And so there’s real worry about that, I think. And then from that follows another liability, which is that Netanyahu, when it comes to actually staying in power and staying out of jail, he’s a man who will not shrink from any bargain. And his coalition partners are not responsible actors by a stretch of anyone’s imagination. So that combination of cynicism on his part and the need to put together small-party coalitions with radical Jewish groups, Orthodox Jewish groups leveraging their small stakes of the overall electorate for outsized gain is very worrying from the point of view of anyone interested in the long-run stability of government there.

Then finally, there’s international isolation that may follow from this. There’s no real appetite in either Europe or the United States to take strong action against Israel. I mean, for heaven’s sake, how much more evidence do you need of that? They’re not on the knife’s edge here. This is not the 1980s, when Israel was in desperate trouble and was seriously actually in the doghouse after its assault on Lebanon. We’re in a different world from that. Nevertheless, the actions of the Netanyahu government and its broader circle notably in the West Bank are beginning to raise heckles. And that’s uncomfortable.

So I think in all of these respects, there’s a sort of preference for the same but just slightly less cynical and slightly less radical and slightly less offensive to global public opinion. And Netanyahu is just personally conflicted because of his legal risks. So that’s why I think there’s that preference there.

CA: In the waning days of the campaign, Netanyahu said that, if reelected, he would prepare Israel to become a “bypass economy” to deal with greater international isolation and sanctions. What might Netanyahu have meant by that exactly?

AT: Yes, it’s an extraordinary stage in Netanyahu’s remarkable career, which starts with him in the ’90s as this strategist of hardening Israel for the arrival of an unthinkable future for which it needs to be prepared, which is the moment where his right-wing vision of Israel’s future, his racially exclusionary vision, requires Israel to make choices that mean that it will face this moment of truth. And what that initially meant was a pattern that we saw across the world in the ’90s and the early 2000s, which is so-called self-insurance. In other words, you switch your fiscal politics into austerity mode, you ran a current account surplus, so you run a trade surplus, you accumulate foreign exchange reserves, and you build a kind of hard-nut capacity that means you can withstand the external pressure. So along with Israel, you might think of China, you might think of [President Vladimir] Putin’s Russia as all following a kind of strategy of this type. Israel obviously is a much smaller country, but huge foreign exchange reserves.

And the question, of course, is when does this get triggered? And because de facto Israel actually enjoys the connivance and support of Europe and the U.S., it isn’t until the current moment that it has begun to get triggered, because the extremity of Netanyahu’s policy since October 2023 is really pushing the envelope of what’s working. And in September 2025, he came out with this extraordinary statement that Israel needed to prepare to be a super Sparta. Which would be a kind of self-contained, hard-knocked, militarized economy that was able to assert its interests. Then of course, you know, things pivoted in its direction. It found that it could manipulate the Trump administration. I think that super-Sparta claim came at the moment when they were having their wrists slapped about their attack against Qatar.

And now we’ve had this bypass thing, which seems to be a kind of idea that somehow Israel’s leadership and key parts of its economy can be insulated from external pressure by essentially bypassing into crypto and using various types of fintech, which Israel has huge strengths in, to bypass sanctions. And it’s a total illusion and it’s no surprise that the responsible financial authorities in Israel, officials at the central bank, said, “What the hell are you talking about, this makes no sense.”

Because Israel is hugely dependent on the outside world for foreign investment, for markets. You know, this is not an economy that can easily cut itself off. Its exports are 60 percent high-tech. It’s business R&D is heavily financed from abroad to the tune of about 47 percent. The venture capital investment in Israel which drives its tech sector last year was over 70 percent from abroad. The idea that you can bypass this through some crypto somehow sneak your way past international tension is just silly. The calm factor of the matter are the numbers that we started with. Over the period since October 2023, the Israeli stock market has boomed. You know, money has flown in, the shekel has been strong. The idea that somehow it’s liable to be punished for anything other than the most egregious actions which somebody might actually finally decide to take criminal action over—it might be a problem for Netanyahu and some of his cronies, but not for Israel as such, right? So there’s a way in which he is dragging Israel into his own maelstrom of increasingly acute legal issues.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

#6079. Iran Is Still a Menace

A member of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at a military training center for citizens in Tehran, Iran, November 2, 2026.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters

The American public may not be interested in the Iran war, but it is still interested in us.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his home to a military base after credible Iranian threats against his life. Bessent helps oversee the crippling financial sanctions imposed on Iran, making him a particular target for the regime.

In the past several years, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Adviser John Bolton, and President Trump himself have also been the targets of Iranian assassination plots.

With the Iran war playing a prominent role in the GOP’s stunning defeat in last week’s elections, there is renewed pressure — both from incoming Democrats and critics on the right — to put an end to the conflict.

On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that JD Vance had become lead negotiator with Iran, to the point of even contemplating direct talks with a top Iranian security official. The same article related that Trump had started to second-guess the wisdom of the June memorandum of understanding that Vance negotiated and that Trump gladly signed, wondering whether it allowed time for Iran to regroup and earn more oil revenue.

On Thursday morning, Trump, who has been vacillating between threatening to bomb Iran and touting imminent peace almost by the day, poured cold water on the idea of any renewed negotiations. The president took to Truth Social to say that he was asking Vance to focus on corruption in Democrat-run cities. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Bombast aside, a status quo in which the U.S. maintains a naval blockade against Iran and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz may be the least bad of the remaining options. While maintaining that pressure, the U.S. should also look for ways to actively support the Iranian opposition, something President Trump implicitly promised in January with his “help is on its way” comments. But we obviously cannot bank on the Iranian regime falling or moderating any time soon. It is hard to see what can be accomplished strategically through another weeks-long air campaign, but the immediate diplomatic prospects are dim, as well.

Presumably, any deal that Iran would agree to in the aftermath of what it considers its victory in the midterms would be a bad one for the U.S., likely a repeat of Barack Obama’s disastrous Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, if not worse. Under that agreement, Iran enjoyed hundreds of billions of dollars in sanctions relief, preserved its ability to enrich uranium, and maintained its ballistic missile program. The scandal of the Iran deal was that even if it worked exactly as intended, it would have still allowed Iran to continue to develop a more powerful conventional military, to sponsor terrorism, and to exert a malign influence within the region and around the world. All the while, restrictions on its nuclear program were set to expire over time, putting the regime on a long-term glide path to weaponization. If any eventual agreements are to be reached with Iran, they must meet two tests: First, do no harm, and second, trade nothing for any promises of future conduct by the Iranians.

Iran’s plots against one of the most important U.S. cabinet officials, as well as Americans throughout the Middle East, underline the malignity of an Iranian regime that has been in a conflict with the United States for a half century. In short, it is still very interested in the war, and in doing us harm.

#6077. Goodbye from Salon

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

#6075. ‘Sabotage’: Read Hegseth’s Fiery Speech Against His Impeachment

Transcript: ‘Sabotage’: Read Hegseth’s Fiery Speech Against His Impeachment

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a rare press conference on Tuesday morning as he faced the prospect of impeachment, delivering an uncompromising and combative speech in defense of his record while excoriating his political opponents.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president; this country; and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it. It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said at the beginning of his remarks.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a rare press conference on Tuesday morning as he faced the prospect of impeachment, delivering an uncompromising and combative speech in defense of his record while excoriating his political opponents.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president; this country; and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it. It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said at the beginning of his remarks.

The impeachment effort, led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, largely focuses on the Defense Department chief’s central role in the Iran war but also pertains to other major military actions under his watch—including strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats near Latin America and the operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Massie, who introduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary on Monday, accuses Hegseth of waging war against Iran without congressional approval, abusing the powers of his office, and violating federal law and the Constitution.

The House is scheduled to hold an initial procedural vote on impeachment on Tuesday evening.

Below is the full transcript of Hegseth’s speech.—John Haltiwanger

Well, good morning. I’ll get right to it. What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president; this country; and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it. It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.

In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that. Not once, war powers resolution or not. Not under [former U.S. President Ronald] Reagan in Lebanon, not under [former U.S. President Bill] Clinton in Kosovo, not under [former U.S. President Barack] Obama in Iraq and Syria, not under [former U.S. President Joe] Biden in Iraq and Syria. That’s the standard. The history is clear, and it’s very straightforward. And one disgruntled congressman wants to shred it over policy disagreements. That’s what it is: policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.

The proper remedy for a policy disagreement—it’s legislation, it’s debate, it’s the next presidential election. It’s not handing the House and Senate floor to the Democrats so that they can run a show trial against the president and the secretary of war while Republicans still control Congress and should be delivering wins for the American people. You see, we’ve seen this show before. They impeached [U.S.] President [Donald] Trump over a perfect phone call. They impeached him again in his final week in office. Both times they failed. Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House.

Now, they’re trying a third time. This time against a member of his cabinet. They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.

Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies—Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching—that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations. It tells them that a single rogue legislator, loaded with personal animus for the president, can attempt to veto national security decisions made by the duly elected commander in chief. It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time. This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.

You know, five years ago, America was humiliated in Kabul, Afghanistan, and every enemy on earth took notice. But somehow, as the president pointed out yesterday—no impeachment vote for [former U.S. Defense Secretary] Lloyd Austin for that terrible withdrawal. Not even one vote. Or no impeachment vote for when he went AWOL for over a week. No impeachment vote for when he let a Chinese spy balloon fly over the country for over a week. See, President Trump ended that kind of wokeness and weakness. Peace through strength, not as a slogan, but as a way of war.

The Houthis found out first. They fired on American ships. Biden had let it happen. President Trump said, “no more.” Operation Rough Rider hit them more than 1,000 times. They cried uncle, and they stopped shooting at our ships to this day. Iran found out next. Operation Midnight Hammer, B-2s from the heartland, halfway around the world, straight into Fordow, Natanz, and Esfahan—flawless. The largest and most successful B-2 strike in American history. Nuclear sites obliterated.

Later in Operation Epic Fury, by every measure, we achieved a historic military victory. Under 40 days of sustained combat, more than 13,000 targets struck. Their navy sunk, their air force grounded, their defense industrial base gone, more than 80 percent of their nuclear industrial base gone, their military in ruin, the ironclad blockade unbroken. We control the Strait of Hormuz. Crazy Islamists in Tehran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. A historic effort, only made possible by a courageous commander in chief. History will judge the Iran war quite differently than conventional wisdom right now. We didn’t start this war; Iran did, 47 years ago.

But President Trump is willing to do what no other president would. He did the tough, right thing—not for politics, but for the safety and the security of the American people. That’s leadership.

He did not kick the can; he kicked their teeth in. For generations—my generation fought other Middle Eastern wars that dragged on for years, for decades. We lost thousands, thousands of Americans. I wear the bracelet of one of them on my left wrist every single day. It reminds me.

And may I remind you, for perspective, we lost 60,000 Americans in Vietnam over 20 years. We lost 37,000 in Korea in just three years. That many humans are lost on the front lines of Ukraine and Russia every month. This—Epic Fury—has never been that, and it never will be. The media can just never admit the military success because they, you, hate the president more than you love our country or our troops.

Then, in our own hemisphere, we started at home from day one. President Trump made homeland security national security. We sent American troops to lock down the southwest border and choked off the cartel pipeline of human smuggling, of drugs, and death. And then, we took the fight to them. The cartels thought they could just poison the American people and hide from justice. So we formed a counter-cartel coalition, designated them terrorists, and hunted them at sea, and now on land. More than 70 narco-vessels sunk; 218 narcoterrorists dead, where they should be; maritime smuggling down at least 65 percent and dropping even further. Thousands of American lives saved with every drug boat sunk and every shipment prevented.

Indicted and wanted, Nicolás Maduro thought he was untouchable. He was not kidnapped. He was brought to justice by America’s best. Victory in one night. Victory in 48 minutes, to be precise. And today, he sits in front of an American judge in New York City. Flawless success.

Panama kicked China’s Belt and Road Initiative to the curb, and we, along with them, control the canal. The message is simple: This is our hemisphere. Act accordingly.

Our NATO allies, after decades of riding on the American taxpayer in Europe, committed to 5 percent of GDP for their own defense. Our allies are finally stepping up. Out with being a burden, in with burden sharing. Why? Because President Trump demanded it. America is the only country on Earth, and this military the only one, that could successfully execute and lead all of these operations and efforts. Sheer success, victories in both Venezuela and Iran, energy security in our hemisphere, in a way none thought possible for a generation, and no nuclear bomb for Iran ever.

But of course, security doesn’t come free. Nobody was lost in the mission in Venezuela, but 18 Americans have given their lives in Operation Epic Fury. We know their names. I’ve been to Dover. We honor them every day, but their sacrifice only stiffens our resolve.

As it happens, tomorrow is Veterans Day. This year, the operators of Absolute Resolve and the warriors of Epic Fury will mark it for the first time. They stand shoulder to shoulder with the pilots of Midnight Hammer and the sailors of Rough Rider who went before them. They answered the call, they executed, they won, and on the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime.

Their service was not a crime. These are heroes, and no politician in Washington will tell them otherwise while I hold this office. President Trump gave this department what it has not had in a generation: a commander in chief with the courage to lead and the resolve to win. I stand behind every one of these operations, I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.

And while this defeated politician—defeated ironically by a Navy SEAL, I might add—while this defeated politician drafts articles of impeachment, we’ve delivered the first increase, and a big one, in hostile fire and imminent danger pay in more than 20 years. We’ve reinstated over 600 service members who were forced out under the previous administration’s COVID[-19] mandate. All five of our services broke historic recruiting records: the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Space Force, the Marines for two years in a row. In fact, the Marines in FY27 met half of their goal on day one. Americans are lining up to serve in President Trump’s Department of War. And by the way, to those Marines and all those Marines out there, semper fi and happy 251st birthday today.

Two years of historic recruitment after Biden couldn’t recruit anyone. Same with retention, by the way, through the roof. That means the troops that are in are staying in. The best of the best, based on merit, staying in. Night and day from Biden to Trump. We cut unnecessary senior officer billets by 20 percent and raised combat performance standards. Through the One Big Beautiful Bill, we’re investing in troop pay, in housing, in healthcare, in advanced weapons and equipment our warfighters actually need to win. That’s the record. That’s what we’re defending.

Make no mistake about what is happening. This is not about me. Politicians in Washington have accused the sailors and the pilots who struck narcoterrorist boats of war crimes for doing their job. Senators in cute videos have suggested the same. This resolution is the next step. Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow. If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me.

As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen. Every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs. We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco-dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s the job well done.

For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America’s military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them. Condemned not for defeat, but for military victory. The disgruntled congressman even admitted this himself yesterday. No failure here, just impeachment for success.

As to the claim that the American military targets civilians, well, that is a lie and that is a slander against every professional who flew, sailed, and fought on these missions. The only people who target civilians are the terrorists that we hunt, and I will dignify this claim no further. None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors; they’re partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military.

We will not apologize for putting American lives first. We will not apologize for stopping the flow of drugs that kill our citizens. We will not apologize for destroying the capabilities of a regime that chants “Death to America,” and if that regime makes one wrong move, as the president said, we remain locked and loaded with the full weight and lethality of Central Command. We will not apologize for restoring a military that recruits based on merit, restores real standards, and fights to win.

These resolutions are a farce. They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders. This process hands our adversaries a propaganda victory and wastes the time of Congress that should instead be focused on protecting the American people.

We will continue to do the job the American people elected President Trump to do: protect this country, defeat our enemies, and rebuild a military worthy of the warriors who wear the uniform.

I pray each day, and I hope you do too, for our troops. They are the best of our nation. Like the president, I will defend them with every fiber of my being, every single day. That includes having their back, no matter what. So to the troops, as I’ve said before: Don’t blink, ignore the noise, never hesitate. This is all politics. You do real things. Stay the course. May Almighty God protect them always, and may our actions today and every day bring glory to Him. We will stand, we will fight, and we will defend this republic against all enemies, foreign and domestic. And amen.

#6072. The Week: Jensen Huang, Honeytrapped

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks with the media ahead of a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., December 3, 2025.

• China has gained an edge in one of the world’s most dangerous technologies: the honeypot.

• Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the tech giant Nvidia, as news of extramarital affairs with multiple subordinates and a spy scandal engulfed the company. The “other woman” in the honeytrap has been identified in numerous reports as a Chinese national and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company in the business of renting out computing power that relies on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities). U.S. intelligence has accused Megaspeed of smuggling contraband chips to China and identified the Nvidia CEO’s paramour as a Chinese spy, information that was passed on to senior officials in Washington. The FBI and Congress are taking a closer look. Nvidia’s advanced chips are absolutely critical for cutting-edge AI models, so handling this scandal will be complicated. We are ahead of China in the AI “arms race” to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

#6071. There’s Never a New Middle East

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: There’s Never a New Middle East

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

This year’s op-eds and magazine features induce déjà vu. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was supposed to clear the way for a new, democratic Middle East. The 2006 Lebanon War was, in U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice’s phrase, the “birth pangs” of a new Middle East. The Arab Spring in 2009 was its dawn. Hamas’s assault on Israel in 2023 was said to be ushering in a new Middle East.

The U.S. attacks on Iran and the fight over the Strait of Hormuz are said to be bringing yet another one into being. Per U.S. President Donald Trump, “The Middle East will be transformed, and the future of that region has never—I don’t think it’s ever looked brighter.” Foreign Affairs weighed in with an article titled “The Iran Imperative: How America and Israel Can Shape a New Middle East.”

This year’s op-eds and magazine features induce déjà vu. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was supposed to clear the way for a new, democratic Middle East. The 2006 Lebanon War was, in U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice’s phrase, the “birth pangs” of a new Middle East. The Arab Spring in 2009 was its dawn. Hamas’s assault on Israel in 2023 was said to be ushering in a new Middle East.

The U.S. attacks on Iran and the fight over the Strait of Hormuz are said to be bringing yet another one into being. Per U.S. President Donald Trump, “The Middle East will be transformed, and the future of that region has never—I don’t think it’s ever looked brighter.” Foreign Affairs weighed in with an article titled “The Iran Imperative: How America and Israel Can Shape a New Middle East.”

Bloody and chaotic events like the Iran war induce fantasies of comprehensive change, but reality keeps coming up short. As Sam Rayburn, House speaker in an earlier era observed: “Any jackass can kick down a barn, but it takes a carpenter to build one.” Decisive change for the better—in the United States’ conception—demands an actual preponderance of U.S. military power and the ability to convert that power into enduring political arrangements. The United States has imagined itself as wielding both attributes while possessing neither.

The use of force halfway around the world requires political leaders to show that the stakes are commensurate with the cost and risk. That means war aims are framed in extravagant terms that are eventually revealed as detached from quotidian reality.

On the other side, adversaries have agency. They are not passive objects of U.S. power projection or a substrate onto which Washington can project its fantasies. And, ironically, the weakness and fragmentation of regional states makes it more, not less, difficult for an outside power to impose its will.

When the war ends, as it eventually will, Iran will still be a poor, militarized oil exporter with two good friends—China and Russia—and a strong relationship with Iraq. In short, not terribly different than it was before the war.

Iraq will look much as it does now, a state with a hybrid army trying to fend off pressure from Iran, with which it shares a long border, and from the United States, which controls its finances.

Syria will look as it did the day before the United States and Israel struck Iran. It will be poor, shattered by 13 years of civil war and many more of sanctions, run by a sectarian clique, penetrated by outside powers from Turkey to Israel and Saudi Arabia, and still riven by ethnic and religious rivalries.

Lebanon will still be living with the results of the 1989 Taif Accord, which ended Lebanon’s civil war by rebalancing power among its sects and calling for every militia to disarm. Under Syrian tutelage, every militia did except Hezbollah, which kept its guns as “the resistance.” This, in turn, inadvertently but predictably locked in Hezbollah’s status as an armed rival to the state and a picker of pointless fights with its far more powerful neighbor to the south. It will still be engaged in the Sisyphean task of satisfying the International Monetary Fund (IMF) without a parliament willing to decide who absorbs the banking system’s losses.

Egypt, whose economy suffered badly when the Houthis were firing on ships in the Red Sea two years ago, will still be the same authoritarian state, propped up by Gulf largesse and embarked on gigantic infrastructure projects, that it was the day before the war.

Jordan, necessarily careful given the mayhem on its Israeli, Syrian, and Iraqi borders, will look exactly as it did before the war. So, too, will Libya, Morocco, Algeria, and Sudan—which will all be what they were last year and the year before that.

True, there is the odd beneficiary. The largely unrecognized country of Somaliland has collected strategic rent from the UAE, Israel, and the United States as a geographical counterweight to Houthi domination of the Bab el-Mandeb. But one breakaway enclave doth not a new Middle East make.

What about the Arab side of the Gulf? Every state there has been pummeled by Iranian missiles and drones. Every Gulf state but Oman will see its economy shrink this year. The IMF projects contractions of 16.7 percent for Kuwait, 15.6 percent for Qatar, 11.3 percent for Bahrain, and smaller ones for the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The IMF expects a sharp rebound next year, but only on the generous assumption that traffic through the strait returns to normal during 2027. Crude flows are already at prewar levels even if the process of moving it is cumbersome.

Most of these states are talking about huge new pipeline or transportation projects, whether from Abqaiq to Yanbu, Habshan to Fujairah, or Basra to Baniyas, to make their export routes redundant and therefore more resilient to Iranian or Houthi attacks. Plans for such projects are nothing new for them, and most will probably never be built. All will rush to rebuild their own air defenses now that the United States has shown itself to be relatively ineffectual as a wager of wars but still an eager arms dealer, source of intelligence, and defense industrial partner. This won’t have a significant effect on their militaries, which, except for the UAE, do not have an expeditionary function, but it will improve their resilience in the face of future Iranian and Houthi attacks.

How does this war end? One way is for the Trump administration to sign a concessionary cease-fire that restores normal traffic through the strait and frees the U.S. Navy to redeploy. A Democratic U.S. Congress could hasten that choice. It would not stop the war outright, since Trump would veto a war powers resolution, and Democrats would likely lack the votes to override him.

A fight over funding would still make the war harder to sustain but hand Trump a win-win situation. Instead of going down as the president who lost the war he started, he could blame the loss on Democrats. The Gulf states would then fall back on their traditional, prudent, and strategy of hedging. They would strike side deals with Iran to fully open the strait while holding onto as much U.S. intelligence, technology, weaponry, and expertise as they can, even if the Fifth Fleet were no longer headquartered in Bahrain.

This would look a lot like the over-the-horizon posture—whereby the United States keeps its forces just outside the region, mostly at sea and at a few access points, and relies on prepositioned equipment and basing rights to surge in a crisis instead of stationing large forces on land. This stance served a strategy of offshore balancing, which kept the United States out of a region’s day to day, intervening only when a single power threatened to dominate a region that it considers vital.

The other way is that the war does not end, at least not soon. This seems to be the outcome that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth prefer, and on its own terms, it is working. Bessent’s satellite imagery shows no tankers at Kharg Island, and Gulf crude, moving under U.S. escort, is leaving the region at or above prewar volumes.

Why settle? Because Iran gets a vote. A strategy of economic attrition gives Tehran every reason to show that the attrition will cost Washington more than it is willing to pay. That is the purpose of the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, the attacks at Dhahran and Dammam, and the threats against U.S. bases. Since the midterm elections, the president has been signaling a disinclination to escalate pending the outcome of talks with Iran, while insisting that the blockade will continue. This in turn will leave the door open for Iranian attacks on shipping that could prompt the escalation Trump is seeking to avoid. A third carrier group is on its way, ensuring that he will have the combat power he needs to follow through.

If the war does drag on, something will change, though not in the way that the prophets of a new Middle East intend. When the Theodore Roosevelt arrives in the Arabian Sea, three quarters of the Navy’s deployed carriers will be allocated to the war. With the arrival of the Roosevelt in the Andaman Sea, there is now no U.S. carrier in the Western Pacific. A region that absorbs this much U.S. power is changing the United States’ position in Asia. The Middle East is remaking U.S. strategy, rather than the other way around.

The only other major player is Israel. For years, observers have noted the rightward drift of Israeli politics, the collapse of left-wing parties, a more militant posture toward the region, tense relations with the United States, hardening opposition to a two-state solution, and the development of a long-range strike capability meant to disable Iran’s nuclear and missile programs and, as it turned out, to kill many of its leaders. This trend was likely to end in war sooner or later; but it was Hamas’s late leader, Yahya Sinwar, who pushed the button.

The result has been catastrophic for Gazans and for Palestinians more generally. It drove Israeli forces across the borders of Syria and Lebanon and created the widespread impression that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lured Trump into the war. These events have accelerated the souring of American opinion about Israel and the U.S.-Israeli relationship in ways that were anticipated a decade ago—particularly the narrowing of political support for the relationship and its transformation into partisan football—well before the current Gulf War began.

This latest pointless war has demonstrated both the persistent American desire for a new Middle East and the inability to make it happen. The 2016 and 2024 U.S. elections were, in part, a referendum on U.S. interventions in the region. Trump appeared to understand that and made it part of his pitch: “I’m not going to start a war,” he declared in 2024, “I’m going to stop wars.”

But restraint has never really been his lodestar, as long as others were footing the bill and he could posture as a warlord. That’s too bad for dead Iranian schoolgirls, U.S. soldiers, and families back home struggling with war-induced inflation.

As for a new Middle East, let alone a better one, the experiment to run is not to test yet again whether military intervention leaves the region better off, since the answer to that is known, but whether less intervention does so.

That experiment is likely to be run by the next U.S. administration, which will answer to a public that sees the Iran war as a mistake, a gratuitous return to the military adventurism that voters repudiated in 2008. Colossal debt and demand for spending on the lives of ordinary people will squeeze the defense budget. Congress, for better or worse, will be looking to the security of the Western Pacific and Europe first. The Middle East will have survived a great deal of American help. It may yet survive less of it.

Steven Simon is a distinguished fellow and visiting professor at Dartmouth College and the author of Grand Delusion: The Rise and Fall of American Ambition in the Middle East. He spent 20 years in the U.S. government, holding senior positions in the State Department and at the National Security Council. He is a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. X: @sns_1239

#6068. U.S.-Mediated Russia-Ukraine Talks Make Little Headway

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: U.S.-Mediated Russia-Ukraine Talks Make Little Headway

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government.

Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government.

Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue.

Tuesday’s conversations were “constructive and quite substantive,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who did not attend the talks, wrote on Telegram. Lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky similarly expressed hope that this week’s dialogue will “allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”

But while negotiators are projecting cautious optimism, neither side appears willing to make concessions, and significant breakthroughs remain out of reach.

Two key sticking points continue to hamper the ongoing peace talks. Ukraine and its European allies insist on an immediate cease-fire before negotiating a wider settlement; Russia, however, rejects such a truce, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arguing that Brussels is just trying to “buy time” for Kyiv. Ukraine also opposes any demands for it to cede territory to Russia, whereas Moscow wants Kyiv to withdraw from the four Russian-occupied regions of the Donbas.

“Nobody believes that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will stop if we leave the Donbas,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday. “He will pause. And then he will return in a year, two, or five years. And who will be to blame?”

Battle lines have not changed substantially in recent months, and just hours before negotiations began in Abu Dhabi, Russia launched overnight attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing outages in six regions. Moscow has repeatedly targeted Kyiv’s power grid in an effort to freeze Ukraine into submission ahead of what is expected to be another cold winter.

But outside pressures could force Moscow and Kyiv to ramp up peacemaking efforts. Prolonged fighting has strained Russia’s wartime economy, Ukraine’s weapons arsenal remains dangerously low on U.S.-made interceptors, and European nations appear increasingly focused on addressing Black Sea security concerns. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged $56 million to help Bulgaria and Romania launch a Black Sea maritime security hub in the face of deadly drone attacks on cargo ships.

Despite these influences, the likelihood of an imminent peace deal appears to be slim. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday during the G-7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris. “It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.”

Hegseth fights back. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a defiant rebuttal on Tuesday of bipartisan efforts to impeach him for “high crimes and misdemeanors” related to his execution of the Iran war, deadly strikes on alleged drug boats, and capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said, referring to outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who has led the impeachment push against him on the grounds that Hegseth has abused his power and endangered members of the armed forces.

The defense secretary went on to defend his policy decisions, champion military recruitment, and characterize the proceedings as a direct attack on the armed forces. “These resolutions are a farce,” Hegseth said. “They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders.”

The comments, made during Hegseth’s first news conference at the Pentagon in six months, came just hours before the House of Representatives was scheduled to hold an initial procedural vote on the impeachment articles.

Still, the Trump administration is not shying away from the fight. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday.

Deadlocked coalition talks. The Israeli Knesset swore in its new lawmakers on Tuesday, just days after President Isaac Herzog tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government. “You must do everything to avoid a repeat election,” Herzog told lawmakers during the swearing-in ceremony. But with coalition-building efforts still deadlocked, Israel’s incoming parliamentary term could be cut short if both Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fail to form a governing bloc.

Eisenkot’s fragmented opposition has the backing of 67 members in the 120-seat Knesset, compared to Netanyahu’s 46 supporters. However, Eisenkot’s path to power remains uncertain, as many of his mainstream Jewish partners have balked at the idea of entering into a formal alliance with Arab-led parties. Without the latter group’s 19 seats, Eisenkot’s bloc lacks the 61-seat majority that it needs to solidly oppose Netanyahu. But with them, Eisenkot could be risking his long-term political future; the only time that an Israeli governing coalition has included an Arab-led party, the alliance held together for just a little more than a year.

In the meantime, Eisenkot has already vowed to replace the Knesset’s speaker, Amir Ohana. Ohana is a Netanyahu loyalist, so removing him would deal a significant blow to the right wing’s legislative agenda. The opposition hopes to replace him with Matan Kahana, a senior figure in Eisenkot’s party, but the date for such a vote has yet to be determined.

Spotty record. The United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC) agreed on Tuesday to further delay a regular review of the United States’ human rights record after Washington was set to become the first U.N. member to fully reject it. The process will now reconvene in January.

Every four to five years, the world’s top human rights body examines the records of all 193 U.N. member states to determine whether governments are adhering to international human rights standards. According to a new report by the office of the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, the United States appears to have violated several of these norms, from targeting civilian infrastructure in Iran to imposing sanctions on the International Criminal Court that “could undermine accountability for war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

The White House pulled out of the council last year, alleging anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and it has repeatedly skipped its HRC review appointments. “[W]e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson told The Associated Press, calling the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values.’”

The Booker Prize for fiction was awarded on Monday to The End of Everything, a dystopian satirical novel by British writer M. John Harrison that explores how difficult it is to understand a deteriorating world when you are right in the middle of it. This was the first time that the prestigious award went to a bona fide science fiction writer, though Harrison maintains that the recognition signals how the era of “genres as fences and boxes, pigeonholes, is over.”

British fantasy and science fiction is having something of a moment in literary prizes, FP’s James Palmer told World Brief. Harrison’s disciple, China Miéville, recently won the prestigious Goldsmiths Prize for his more than 1,200-page paranormal Cold War epic The Rouse.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#6066. What Progressives Could Do on Israel

Report: What Progressives Could Do on Israel

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Riding high on the midterm elections’ blue wave, progressive Democrats feel they have the momentum to push through major changes to Washington’s support for Israel.

“What you are looking at behind me is a mandate,” U.S. Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, who is a Democratic Socialist, said at a Sunday press conference introducing the new progressive House lawmakers. “It is a mandate from the American people to unrig our economy … to tax the rich, to abolish [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], and to end the genocide” in Gaza.

Riding high on the midterm elections’ blue wave, progressive Democrats feel they have the momentum to push through major changes to Washington’s support for Israel.

“What you are looking at behind me is a mandate,” U.S. Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, who is a Democratic Socialist, said at a Sunday press conference introducing the new progressive House lawmakers. “It is a mandate from the American people to unrig our economy … to tax the rich, to abolish [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], and to end the genocide” in Gaza.

Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson have also described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide,” while Sen.-elect James Talarico has called for “stopping offensive weapons sales” to the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

El-Sayed told NPR after his election win: “I’d also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel.” And Jackson, who has called Netanyahu a “war criminal,” said in a September interview with a local Maine news station that he doesn’t want the United States sending a “blank check” to the Israeli government anymore.

“I’m not willing to vote for any more bombs, any more aid going [to Israel],” Jackson said at a candidate event in September.

A bill that has already drawn significant progressive Democratic support is the Block the Bombs Act, which would forbid the transfer to Israel of some of the most destructive bombs in the U.S. arsenal, such as so-called bunker-buster bombs. The legislation has attracted more than 80 co-sponsors, and while it has no chance of passing the House this year, it is seen as a good candidate for being reintroduced next year with even more momentum behind it.

“The Block the Bombs Act has been a tremendous organizing vehicle that went further than many of us even thought,” said Hassan El-Tayyab, the legislative director for Middle East policy at the Quaker lobby group Friends Committee on National Legislation, adding that he would “definitely” like to see progressives go further and try to ban even more weapons than the seven munitions listed in the legislation.

Beyond the progressive wing of the incoming freshman class of Democratic lawmakers, many other Democrats with more centrist backgrounds were elected to the House and Senate or are predicted to win their still uncalled races.

But underlining just how far leftward the terrain of the policy debate has shifted among even centrist Democrats is Eileen Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral who served on the National Security Council during the Biden administration. Laubacher, who is on the verge of flipping a red Colorado district, has said U.S. foreign aid to Israel should end, as “Israel has the ability to pay for their own weapons for defense.” However, she believes that the country should be allowed to continue to purchase U.S. weapons on a “case-by-case basis.”

Still, those newly elected progressive and centrist lawmakers won’t be seated until January. And with the 2028 U.S. presidential contest already starting to shape up, the pressure is on for would-be Democratic nominees “to show that they are meeting a new moment in the party,” said Akbar Shahid Ahmed, the author of Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza.

Which means we could see some policy moves before the new Congress is even sworn in.

Israel’s backers in Congress this summer included a provision in the must-pass annual defense policy bill directing the Pentagon to increase the role of Israeli technologies in the development of new weapon systems. Backers hope the provision will lead to further integration of the U.S. and Israeli defense industries for years to come.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith, who is poised to resume the chairmanship of the House Armed Services Committee, has said he would support removing the language from the bill. A compromise version of the massive bill is being hammered out by Senate and House staff and is likely to be presented to lawmakers for a vote on final passage in the next few weeks.

El-Tayyab said he is watching to see if Smith and other Democrats are willing to vote against the entire defense policy bill and risk potentially killing its chances of passage this year if the Israeli technology provision isn’t removed.

“The question is, will they go all the way and refuse to give it the support it needs to pass if that provision remains in there?” El-Tayyab said.

Meanwhile, if recent history is any predictor, there’s a good chance lawmakers will be unable to finish work on fiscal 2027 spending legislation this year. If that happens, then Democrats in January would gain new leverage in the final shaping of the appropriations bills when they take control of the Senate and House. That opens new possibilities for progressives to try to decrease or place limitations on the $3.8 billion in annual security assistance that the United States provides to Israel.

“Given what Donald Trump [said on Nov. 3], what Netanyahu has already said, where the bulk of the caucus is—Republican as well as Democratic—we are headed quickly towards zero financing of American taxpayer subsidies for Israeli arms purchases,” Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of J Street, a liberal pro-Israel U.S. lobbying group, said in a Thursday press call on the results of the midterms. “The bigger legislative battle will be over what are the conditions placed on Israel if it wants to buy weapons.”

Rachel Oswald is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @OswaldRachel

#6064. Texas Democrats put DEI back on agenda after sweeping to power

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, discusses the 2026 midterm election results after Democrats flipped a Texas U.S. Senate seat and won the governor’s race on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’

Texas Democrats are opening their incoming state House majority with a push to clear the way for DEI offices and programs to return to public universities across the state — a move state Republicans are expected to block but that puts the culture-war issue front and center after massive Democratic Party gains in the state.

HB 358 and SB 125 would repeal a 2023 law banning diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) offices and programs at public universities, but the bills face steep odds with Republicans still retaining control of the Texas Senate. Still, the effort signals Democrats’ broader intent to roll back one of the GOP’s signature education policies after campaigning heavily on the war in Iran, immigration and affordability.

Even if the repeal effort fails, conservative policy experts in Texas warn that Democratic appointments to university governing boards could weaken enforcement of the state's DEI restrictions without changing the law.

"With Republicans in firm control of the Texas state Senate, it’s highly unlikely that any bill seeking to bring back the corrosive and wasteful higher ed DEI regime will make it to the Governor’s desk," Chuck DeVore, chief national initiatives officer for the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF), told Fox News Digital. "What will likely happen is that relabeled and disguised DEI programs and classes will make a comeback over the next four years as the Governor’s board of regents appointees gradually get a majority. We look forward to suing to ensure adherence to Texas law."

FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE

University of Texas students walk through campus on the first day of classes on Monday, Aug. 25, 2025. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

The 2023 anti-DEI law, signed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, barred public universities from maintaining DEI offices or assigning employees or contractors to perform their duties. It also prohibited compelling or soliciting DEI statements from faculty or students, restricted certain preferences based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin and banned mandatory DEI training for students and employees. The law includes exceptions for academic instruction, scholarly research and registered student organizations.

After the law took effect Jan. 1, 2024, UT Austin closed its Multicultural Engagement Center and discontinued its Monarch program, which provided advising, mental-health support and scholarships to illegal immigrants and other noncitizen students. The University of Houston System stopped requiring DEI statements in hiring and promotions, while UT Health San Antonio ended a faculty loan-repayment program for professors from "underrepresented backgrounds."

VP VANCE TOUTS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S DISMANTLING OF DEI

At a May 2024 Texas Senate higher education subcommittee hearing, UT System Chancellor J.B. Milliken told lawmakers the system had closed 21 DEI offices, eliminated 311 full- and part-time positions focused on DEI and canceled 681 contracts, programs and training sessions. Critics have nevertheless accused some universities of preserving DEI initiatives under different names or organizational structures.

Texas A&M University drew scrutiny after dissolving its Office for Diversity but transferring six of its eight employees to other campus positions. Former Vice President for Diversity Annie McGowan received a 10% raise, a new position and nine months of paid leave. Critics accused the university of preserving DEI operations under different titles. Texas A&M maintained that the office and its DEI-related duties had been eliminated and that the raises were unrelated to DEI.

Activists hold signs during a news conference about diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) outside the U.S. Capitol on July 23, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Kate Bierly, a higher education campaign director at TPPF, told Fox News Digital that Democrats could undermine Texas' 2023 anti-DEI law without repealing it. She warned that newly appointed university regents could weaken enforcement through administrative inaction, potentially allowing prohibited practices to resume.

She observed that numerous university regents' terms expire Feb. 1, 2027, giving Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa an opportunity to nominate replacements who could influence how universities enforce the DEI ban.

CONGRESS TO PUT AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION IN HOT SEAT OVER DEI RULES TIED TO LAW SCHOOL ACCREDITATION

But Hinojosa would face another obstacle: Republican control of the Texas Senate, which must confirm university regent appointments. Bierly said the Texas Constitution allows certain unpaid gubernatorial appointees, including regents, to remain in office after their terms expire. Because the 90th Legislature convenes in January 2027, before the regents' terms expire, she said incumbents could remain in place until the end of the 91st Legislature's regular session in 2029 if their successors are not confirmed.

The State Capitol is seen in Austin, Texas, on June 1, 2021. (AP Photo/Eric Gay, File)

"If the Senate declines to confirm nominees who would undermine the state's DEI reforms, existing regents can continue serving rather than automatically surrendering their seats when their terms expire," Bierly said. "This holdover period ends on the last day of the first regular legislative session that begins after the term expires. So as a result, the current regents can hold over to 2029 if no successor has qualified by then. After that, the office becomes vacated."

DeVore said the holdover provision could become a political liability for Senate Republicans, giving Democrats "an actual useful campaign cudgel" if the chamber refuses to confirm Hinojosa's nominees. Democrats could accuse Republicans of obstructing the governor's appointments to university governing boards, he said.

That pressure could force a compromise at some point, DeVore added, but also warned that DEI is "a death issue for a Republican primary" and that any Republican who supports a compromise could be "toast in the primary."

State Representative Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat from Texas and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a campaign event with State Representative James Talarico, a Democrat from Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, not pictured, at the Stubbs - Waller Creek Amphitheater in Austin, Texas, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Texas' restrictions reflect a broader national effort to dismantle DEI programs in government and higher education.

The Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling against race-based admissions preferences at universities preceded a broader federal crackdown on DEI. After returning to office in 2025, President Donald Trump moved to dismantle DEI programs across the federal government and directed federally funded schools to end race-based preferences in admissions, hiring, scholarships and other programs.

Republican-led states have pursued similar restrictions at public universities, making Texas’ fight part of a broader national backlash against institutional DEI.

Texas Democrats are opening their incoming state House majority with a push to clear the way for DEI offices and programs to return to public universities across the state. (fstop123/iStock via Getty Images Plus)

Texas' political landscape has shifted dramatically following Republican election losses. Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Attorney General Ken Paxton are leaving office, while Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, lost his Republican Senate primary to Paxton.

Democrats won the governorship, attorney general's office and a U.S. Senate seat while reclaiming the state House for the first time in more than two decades. Republicans retained control of the state Senate, giving them a potential veto over both the DEI repeal legislation and Hinojosa's university regent nominees.

"Ultimately, Texas lawmakers must decide whether they want the DEI ban to be more than a law on paper," Bierly said. "Protecting the reforms requires attention not only to legislation, but also to the university leadership responsible for implementing it."

Fox News Digital sought comment from the repeal bills' sponsors, Democratic state Rep. John Bucy and Democratic state Sen. José Menéndez, as well as former Republican state Sen. Brandon Creighton, who authored the 2023 anti-DEI law and now serves as chancellor of the Texas Tech University System. None responded before publication. The University of Texas System, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and Texas Students for DEI also did not respond to requests for comment.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

#6062. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I’m certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

“We’re gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We’ll have to see if he’s serious, but I don’t trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election’s lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they’ve been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it’s a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn’t chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

“I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He’s also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It’s not even a result. It’s almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn’t on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan’s election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia’s two-word statement on Election Day: “Lawyer up.”

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?” she said. “They’re going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”
