#6061. Did China Play Jensen Huang?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

China Brief: Did China Play Jensen Huang?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s connections to Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Beijing, exploded into a major scandal this week. On Sunday, he admitted to having an extramarital affair, Nvidia stock dropped, and the company announced it was launching an investigation.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation, is a former executive at Megaspeed—a Singapore-based, China-linked cloud-computing company that is Nvidia’s largest chip customer in Southeast Asia. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in 2023, shortly after the United States under President Joe Biden imposed sweeping chip restrictions on China.

Megaspeed has been under scrutiny since 2024, when the U.S. Commerce Department opened a probe into whether it was diverting Nvidia chips to China. Yet late last year, Jensen Huang convinced U.S. President Donald Trump to allow exports of Nvidia’s advanced H200 chip to China, with the White House taking a 25 percent cut. Many of these chips seem to have been sold to Chinese shell companies.

All of this happened even though both Nvidia and the White House seemingly knew about the risks surrounding Alice Huang for months. Trump administration officials were reportedly warned about her connection to Jensen in a classified memo this spring but took no action. Nvidia, meanwhile, hired a public relations firm specializing in sex scandals last year.

So, how did this happen? It’s possible that Alice Huang is an agent for China’s Ministry of State Security and was tasked with honey trapping Jensen Huang. That would suggest Megaspeed, which has denied all allegations that it engaged in misconduct, was repurposed or even created as a vehicle for intelligence gathering and for illicitly obtaining U.S. chips.

But it’s equally plausible that the relationship came first. Alice Huang’s resume is hard to verify, but she seems to have worked in finance and tech for at least a decade. It wouldn’t be the first time that a billionaire businessman got involved with a younger woman who he convinced himself was a brilliant up-and-comer.

If that is the case, either Chinese intelligence became aware of the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang and pressured her to let them exploit it, or she took it to them herself.

As I have noted before, China’s intelligence apparatus is messy, with multiple competing groups inside the government. That leaves room for outsiders to act as intelligence entrepreneurs. Alice Huang may have been working both Jensen Huang and the Chinese government for her own business edge.

Other questions remain unanswered. One is whether Alice Huang persuaded Jensen Huang to do anything on behalf of the Chinese state that he wouldn’t have done anyway, since Nvidia has a vested interest in access to the Chinese market. That said, Nvidia’s intervention to help halt the Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed looks suspicious. (Megaspeed remains under investigation by the U.S. Justice Department.)

Of course, China also benefits from having a line into White House discussions, and we can’t know what Jensen Huang has told Trump about China behind closed doors. Trump’s China policy has certainly been soft, and he has blithely dismissed this week’s revelations.

But why did the Trump administration disregard the warning from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio about Huang’s connections to Chinese intelligence? And who leaked the story to the press, whether out of patriotic feeling or a desire to disadvantage a rival?

It’s certainly a convenient moment for U.S. politicians to distance themselves from the White House and an increasingly unpopular tech sector. A tougher stance on China may become a distinguishing mark for aspiring Republican leaders. Democrats are also seizing on the news as an example of the White House’s tolerance of corruption and foreign influence, and they will likely push for stronger chip restrictions in the new Congress.

Whatever the outcome of the Huang affair, the state of counterintelligence and cybersecurity under Trump remains dire, underscoring a need for root-and-branch reform.

Marriage registrations drop. China’s demographic crisis remains its biggest long-term problem, and the news keeps getting worse. New data shows marriage registrations falling to an 18-year low for the January-to-September period, with 4.65 million couples tying the knot, a nearly 10 percent drop.

For comparison, the United States sees around 2 million marriages in a full year with a population one-quarter the size of China’s. Childbearing is closely tied to marriage in China, so a low marriage rate also means a low birth rate. Children born outside of marriage and their single mothers still face legal and social obstacles, though their situation has improved in recent years.

Hong Kong dissident receives longer sentence. A Hong Kong court has sentenced Joshua Wong, the imprisoned young activist who became the face of the city’s democracy movement more than a decade ago, to another 10 years for supposed collusion with foreign powers. Wong was due for release in January.

Beijing has an interest in portraying Hong Kong’s democracy activists as tools of outside agents. Wong, however, is a cause célèbre among Western politicians—unlike other equally persecuted dissidents such as Macao’s Au Kam San. If the incoming U.S. Congress chooses to take up human rights issues again, Wong’s case will likely return to the spotlight.

U.S.-China trade truce extended. The U.S.-China trade truce was formally extended by another two months on Monday, running through Jan. 10, 2027. In theory, that leaves room for Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to ink a more permanent deal if they meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week.

Xi is well aware of Trump’s need for some kind of victory, and as a result the Chinese leader is likely to come out ahead in any agreement. Whatever deal they reach may not last long: Domestic political pressure in the United States could blow it up before it is in place, especially in the wake of the Huang case.

Japan squabble deepens. Beijing’s relations with Tokyo remain frozen nearly a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan might be obliged to come to Taiwan’s aid if China invaded the self-ruled island. Even at the provincial level, Chinese officials are competing to look tough on Japan.

That is a perennial popularity-booster with both the Chinese Communist Party and the public, for whom the trauma of Japan’s brutal invasion lingers eight decades on.

Now, flights between the two countries are being slashed. Airlines, mostly Chinese, have scheduled nearly 700,000 fewer seats on China-Japan flights this winter, a drop of around 20 percent compared to last year. Takaichi’s stance remains popular at home, and she may be emboldened if a tougher U.S. policy toward China emerges next year.

#6059. The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

THOMAS WRIGHT is a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He served as the Senior Director for Strategic Planning at the National Security Council during the Biden administration.

The midterm elections mark the beginning of the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential campaign. After two years of debate over the lessons of Kamala Harris’s defeat in the 2024 election, it promises to be one of the most open contests about the future of Democratic policies, including foreign policy, in generations. It also promises to be one of the most consequential. The strategic environment in 2029 is on track to be the most difficult and unforgiving since the height of the Cold War.

Democrats must therefore lay out their ideas early and see how they fare both with voters and against the trajectory of world events. The party is generally split into two camps: centrists who, when it comes to foreign policy, are focused on strategic competition, restoring the United States’ national power, and deepening alliances; and progressives, who propose a more affirmative agenda emphasizing shared challenges and global cooperation. In many ways, this divide has become familiar. But as the second Trump administration continues its project of overturning the post–World War II global order, the debates within each camp are at least as important as the disagreements between them.

If the party’s major foreign policy disagreements—on the future of the international order, on Israel, on artificial intelligence, on China, and on the global economy—are not litigated by prospective candidates, former officials, and prominent thinkers now, and voters are not given the chance to make an informed choice between coherent options, the first year of a Democratic administration could be consumed by indecision and infighting. Democrats must therefore understand where they stand on each of those questions, where centrists and progressives converge, and where the sharpest divisions now lie.

The three Democratic presidents since the end of the Cold War have all made some version of a U.S.-led international order a cornerstone of their foreign policy. But although former President Joe Biden’s rhetoric, with its emblematic “America Is Back” catchphrase, gestured at restoring that order after Trump, Biden did not govern like a restorationist. For the Biden administration, in which I served, the intensifying strategic competition with China and Russia and the onset of shared challenges such as the pandemic marked an external unraveling of the old era that necessitated major changes in U.S. strategy. Biden shifted foreign economic policy away from free trade and globalization toward industrial policy, resilience, and technological leadership, and he pushed back more assertively against Beijing and Moscow than did his Democratic predecessors.

As they reflect on the Biden administration, centrists are actively debating whether a future Democratic administration can restore and reform the U.S.-led international order or whether the United States must adapt to a prolonged period of geopolitical upheaval. For now, the differences are more pronounced in diagnosis than in policy prescriptions. All favor deepening alliances and partnerships, modernizing the military, fixing the defense industrial base, strengthening deterrence, tackling transnational challenges such as global public health, and pursuing hardheaded diplomacy with rivals.

Centrists also agree that Trump has severely weakened U.S. power and institutions, although they remain relatively optimistic about the country’s capacity to recover. But most recognize that the world the next Democratic president would inherit in 2029 is not the world that Biden inherited in 2021. Winning an election will not mean the end of Trumpism. The “America first” movement will likely remain a dominant force in the Republican Party, and the United States’ allies and partners will have to hedge against dramatic shifts in U.S. foreign policy from one election to the next. Even if a Democratic president can rebuild American power and repair damaged institutions, restoring international confidence in the durability of U.S. commitments will be much harder.

The party’s progressives argue that the U.S. foreign policy establishment failed over the past 25 years by pursuing U.S. primacy at all costs. They see the U.S.-led order as deeply flawed in its design and track record, arguing that Washington’s selective application of the “rules-based order” undermined the order itself. As Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, put it at the Munich Security Conference in 2026, “In a rules-based order, hypocrisy is vulnerability.” They favor a rules-based order that applies its principles consistently, even if doing so constrains the United States.

Many progressives, led by Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, also believe that a global oligarchy poses a threat to democracy and see big business in defense, technology, and finance as part of a corrupt system. They believe that corporate interests have driven excessive military spending, misguided interventions, and a global economy that favors multinational companies over workers.

Progressives see the turmoil of the past two years as accelerating the emergence of a multipolar order, in which the United States has an important, but more limited, role to play. According to the progressive thinker Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser to President Barack Obama, Washington should “re-engage the world as something other than a hegemon.” Americans are accustomed to seeing the country as an overall force for good, even when it uses military power, but progressives point to U.S. support for Israel’s war in Gaza, and the Trump administration’s actions in Iran and Venezuela as evidence of the enormous damage that interventionism can cause. Many argue that the United States should go to war only in self-defense—and with congressional authorization, as the Constitution requires. They also favor cuts to what they see as a bloated defense budget that encourages presidents to default to military action instead of diplomacy.

Most progressives believe that the greatest threats to American security and prosperity are increasingly transnational rather than geopolitical: runaway artificial intelligence, climate change, and widening inequality, as enumerated by Sanders earlier this year. They argue that the threat from China is often overblown and that deterrence can be achieved and U.S. interests protected with existing capabilities and without a ratcheting up of tensions. As such, most progressives would prioritize cooperation with other powers, especially Beijing, on existential challenges over competition.

A distinct group of thinkers, usually aligned with the progressive camp, identifies with the restraint school of foreign policy. They tend to agree with the centrists about the centrality of geopolitics but want to reduce the United States’ exposure to it. They argue that Washington’s pursuit of military primacy has overstretched the country, unnecessarily embroiling it in conflicts and crises, and favor a more selective approach that focuses on a smaller number of vital interests, reduces overseas commitments, and emphasizes diplomacy, even if it leads to outcomes abroad that conflict with their values.

Despite these differing worldviews, there is much agreement between centrists and progressives. Both camps support NATO, the EU, and Washington’s alliances in the Indo-Pacific. Both want to stand up to Russian President Vladimir Putin and help Ukraine. Both oppose the Iran war and both want to root out corruption. But new debates, both between and within the various camps of the Democratic Party, are steadily emerging alongside those that have historically divided the party.

One of the most important debates currently unfolding in the party is the United States’ relationship with Israel and Washington’s role in the Middle East more generally. This is likely to be the most pronounced break from the Biden administration. Many Democrats blame Biden for not doing enough to restrain Israel in the Gaza war and some former senior Biden administration officials even acknowledge that they should have done more.

Many centrists identify Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the driving force behind a series of Israeli actions that have hurt U.S. interests, such as advocating all-out war against Iran, using excessive force in Gaza, and undermining the Palestinian Authority, and they recommend adjusting U.S. policy accordingly. They believe that Netanyahu’s departure could create an opening for a broader regional settlement, but that Washington would still need to exert pressure on Israel to make progress toward Palestinian statehood. The potential presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel, for instance, has proposed a regional initiative in which the United States would support a Palestinian state in exchange for full Arab recognition of Israel and closer strategic and economic ties across the region. Such an initiative would include forceful U.S. opposition to effective Israeli annexation of the West Bank, backed by sanctions on violent settlers and the entities that build or finance illegal settlements. Emanuel would also end U.S. defense subsidies for Israel, making it purchase weapons on the same terms as other allies.

Other centrists go further. Jon Finer, the former principal deputy national security adviser to Biden, has argued for more sustained pressure on Israel regardless of whether Netanyahu is replaced. The United States must make Israel choose “between the abundant and irreplaceable benefits of the U.S. relationship and the indefensible policies that are driving a wedge between our societies,” Finer wrote recently in The New York Times. This would include treating the occupied territories as different from Israel proper, imposing sanctions on individuals and entities involved in settlement expansion, and conditioning arms sales on Israeli compliance with international humanitarian law.

Few elected Democrats still argue for unconditional support, but a group that emphasizes the value of the U.S.-Israeli alliance and favors lower levels of pressure on Israel will likely remain by 2028. For instance, these centrists would sanction violent settlers, as the Biden administration did, but may not target the banks that finance the construction of new settlements. They would give a new prime minister the benefit of the doubt, should one successfully form a coalition. But if Netanyahu remains in power during the U.S. primary campaign, their position would be hard to sustain.

Many centrists aim to reduce the U.S. military commitment to the Middle East, but they reject the idea of simply walking away from the region. As Philip Gordon, the former national security adviser to Vice President Harris, put it in Foreign Affairs, the United States should “defend a narrower set of core interests with a smaller military footprint, more diplomacy, more alternatives, and more partners.” Centrists are divided over how exactly to do this; some would be open to a defense treaty with Saudi Arabia if it were part of a broader move toward a Palestinian state, whereas others want to avoid new defense commitments. A small group of centrist dissenters, especially those who are primarily concerned about China, see the Middle East as quicksand that stymies U.S. interests in Asia and are more willing to countenance a significant reduction of forces.

Progressives have largely welcomed centrists’ changes on Israel, even if many are skeptical that they would actually follow through on their rhetoric once in power. They tend to see Finer’s support for more sustained pressure on Israel and increased engagement with Palestinians as a good starting point. But many go further. Intraprogressive arguments focus on whether to support Israel’s access to defensive weaponry, such as the Iron Dome missile defense system and whether a Palestinian state should be recognized on day one of a Democratic administration or should be the ultimate goal of a diplomatic initiative. Others favor more radical change. The progressive commentator Peter Beinart, for example, has argued that a two-state solution is no longer viable and progressives should support a single state with equal rights for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis. Some progressives question whether Israel is an ally at all and believe it has little to offer the United States.

More generally, progressives increasingly favor a complete withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Middle East and distancing the United States from its Gulf allies. As Michael Fuchs, Harris’s former deputy chief of staff, wrote in Foreign Affairs, it is “long past time for the United States to withdraw its forces from the Middle East, stop arming governments that violate U.S. and international law, and end its role as guarantor of regional order.”

Israel may be the source of the most contentious division among Democrats, but it is not the only one. AI has also emerged as a source of disagreement, although the battle lines are not so neatly drawn. One group of influential centrists, which includes many Biden administration officials, sees AI as a technology whose benefits are as world-changing as its risks. They believe that the United States must win the race with China—often citing the cyber-capabilities of the Mythos model as an example—but also favor slowing down AI development to ensure that the models are safe and the economic effects, particularly on jobs, can be managed. To do this, they advocate strengthening U.S. export controls over China to provide the breathing room to “pace the frontier” and regulate leading labs. They want to negotiate a common position on AI with allies and partners (including by distributing AI infrastructure to the United States’ closest allies, such as Australia and Canada) and to open a dialogue with China to manage safety risks.

There were, however, significant disagreements within the Biden administration over how to compete technologically with China, which are likely to reemerge in the 2028 campaign. Biden’s Treasury Department questioned whether export controls could prevent China from catching up, arguing that maintaining Chinese dependence on American technology would preserve U.S. leverage and discourage Beijing from developing alternatives. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo shared this skepticism, telling The Wall Street Journal in December 2024 that “trying to hold China back is a fool’s errand,” and that investing in industrial capacity in the United States mattered more than export controls. Other centrist Democrats, such as former National Security Adviser Susan Rice, have argued that the United States and China should negotiate an agreement to freeze AI models in place.

Progressives, meanwhile, are generally unpersuaded that the United States can win, or even needs to win, the frontier race against China. A minority are skeptical of the technology, dismissing the claims of frontier labs as hype, and believe that it can largely be managed with existing legal frameworks. Others, however, believe that the United States should halt AI development, impose a moratorium on new data centers, take an aggressive stance toward the technology companies, and negotiate a grand bargain with China resembling a comprehensive arms control agreement. Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, of California, have both called for a binding agreement with Beijing to restrain the development of potentially dangerous AI systems, explicitly drawing parallels with Cold War nuclear arms control. Progressive members of Congress have mostly voted in favor of export controls on China, although it is unclear whether they would renew and strengthen them if China were to threaten retaliatory escalation early in a new administration.

AI safety could become one of the most consequential issues in the primary, creating new coalitions that cut across the traditional centrist-progressive divide. The pace of AI development and the likelihood of future AI-driven cyberattacks or loss-of-control incidents mean that the issue will remain particularly fluid in the lead-up to 2028.

Several long-standing debates between and within Democratic factions, including on some of the most important issues that the next Democratic president will face, remain unresolved, too. Chief among them is China.

Most centrists see China as the most significant strategic and economic challenge facing the United States, believing that it has a technological and manufacturing lead in many critical areas. They worry about a war over Taiwan but believe it can be avoided if the United States restores its national power, deepens its alliances, strengthens Taiwan’s self-defense and resilience, selectively pushes back against China when necessary, and injects some stability into the relationship through high-level diplomacy—an approach that the Biden administration called “managed competition.” They are actively debating how to expand Biden-era efforts, particularly with respect to alliances and export controls, and how much the United States should dial up its competitive efforts without undermining diplomacy and risking a spiral into confrontation. Although most centrists favor some variant of Biden’s managed competition strategy, some associated with the camp, such as Ryan Hass, who served on Obama’s National Security Council, have cautioned that “attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.”

Progressives see centrists’ strategic competition frame as excessively hawkish and as a self-fulfilling prophecy. They believe that Washington and Beijing have a shared interest in tackling shared challenges, particularly AI safety and climate change and that détente is an achievable goal. Some, including Jessica Chen Weiss, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School for Advanced International Studies who served on the State Department’s Policy Planning staff during the Biden administration, think that Washington should pursue that goal by deepening economic ties with China, ceasing discussion of the strategic competition, and nurturing moderates in the United States and China. Most progressives do not recommend accommodating China’s geopolitical ambitions, but they believe that Washington can reduce the risk of Chinese aggression by exercising restraint and engaging in high-level diplomacy. For progressives, deterrence can be more readily accomplished than centrists believe, both because the United States’ existing military power is sufficient and because China is not an aggressive revisionist power like Russia.

The debate over China is closely linked to another debate over foreign economic policy and trade. Biden’s shift toward industrial policy and supply chain resilience was partly driven by a belief that China’s unfair trading practices merited a fundamental change in U.S. policy. Many centrists now argue for an expansion of industrial policy to cover a wider variety of critical goods, such as robotics. They want to make common cause with Europe to respond to Chinese overcapacity, including by coordinating tariffs and import bans on emerging technologies and by integrating their manufacturing efforts to compete with Beijing. Some, such as the former deputy national security adviser Daleep Singh, have advocated for a sovereign wealth fund to kick-start investment in new technologies. They are perturbed by Trump’s use of coercive economic power against allies and are developing their own doctrine of economic statecraft with appropriate safeguards. Some centrists want to grant allies and partners more access to the U.S. market, not through the expansive multilateral agreements that defined the 1990s and early 2000s but through smaller, more targeted agreements.

There are significant divisions among progressives over the economic threat from China. Elected officials on the left tend to see trade policy toward China very similarly to centrists. Lawmakers such as Khanna, Sanders, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, are also concerned about deindustrialization and China’s dominance of advanced manufacturing and favor stronger measures against Beijing’s unfair trade practices. But progressive foreign policy thinkers are often more skeptical of economic confrontation and favor closer ties with China. Some support industrial policy but are uneasy about framing it principally around competition with China. They recommend pursuing industrial policy for other reasons, such as tackling inequality or climate change, and believe that the United States and China can work together on global economic issues, including Sanders’s proposal for a global minimum wage.

Democrats are likely to disagree on what to do with Trump’s tariffs toward allies and partners, although few talk about it openly. Some say that the next president should describe Trump’s tariffs as an unfair tax on American consumers and lift them immediately and unilaterally. Others may favor keeping some of the tariffs to protect certain industries or as a revenue stream to fund their own domestic priorities. And a third group says that the next administration should lift them as part of a quick negotiation with allies on a common position on economic and technological issues relating to China, including dealing with the overcapacity problem and restoring export controls on China’s compute power.

Different perceptions of China also inform the party’s internecine debates on climate policy. Progressives see climate as one of the top priorities for a new administration, not subordinated to national security goals, and thus prioritize cooperating with China, including on electric vehicles and clean technology. Centrists, however, are skeptical that China will be a reliable climate partner, oppose Chinese electric vehicles on national security grounds, and favor cooperation with smaller groups of like-minded nations as a more dependable way to advance clean technologies.

This disagreement is just one dimension of a deeper split on how best to address climate change. Centrists tend to argue that Democrats should connect climate to affordability, jobs, and energy security rather than making it the organizing principle of the governance agenda. They favor investing in clean technology, although some are more open to natural gas and permitting changes that they say will speed construction. Progressives believe that supporting clean technology is necessary but insufficient and call for policies that reduce the supply of oil and gas.

The centrist-progressive debate runs deeper than a disagreement over policy. It is a question of how the United States can achieve peace and prosperity: by managing geopolitical rivalries and the instabilities stemming from the unraveling of the international order or by overcoming geopolitics through cooperation.

If the party does not have these debates openly and consistently over the next two years, a Democratic president risks entering office in 2029 much as Jimmy Carter did in 1977. Carter inherited an international environment in which the Nixon-Kissinger framework of détente was under increasing strain. His administration was divided between the competing worldviews of National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski, who favored a more confrontational approach to the Soviet Union, and Secretary of State Cyrus Vance, who emphasized diplomacy and arms control. Heated disagreements between the camps repeatedly complicated Carter’s efforts to develop and implement a coherent strategy toward Moscow.

A repeat of the situation in 2029 could be even more damaging. The next president will inherit frayed alliances, mounting Chinese pressure on Taiwan, deepening integration and cooperation among Washington’s adversaries, and potential wars in Iran and Ukraine, not to mention new crises that may emerge over the next two years. Failure to settle on a clear agenda could paralyze U.S. decision-making at precisely the time when a new administration will want to provide strong leadership and direction.

Fortunately, centrists and progressives have considerable common ground. They both are committed to rebuilding the foundations of American power, supporting alliances, backing a just peace in Ukraine, taking transnational challenges seriously, and eschewing unnecessary military interventions. They may not reach a partywide consensus on every issue. But a spirited, productive primary debate will allow voters to make an informed choice and ensure that the first year of the next administration is spent acting on a vision, not arguing over one.

#6058. Pence delivers scathing rebuke of Vance's Iran war assessment, blames Trump policies for GOP losses

Former Vice President Mike Pence, in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview, disputes Vice President Vance’s take on GOP losses, points to what he calls 'self-dealing' and 'air of corruption' in Trump second term.

EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence delivered a blistering assessment of Vice President JD Vance's midterm election postmortem that the war in Iran cost Republicans control of Congress, with the former vice president contending that Americans grew frustrated not because President Donald Trump launched the conflict, but because his administration failed to finish it.

Pence, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, his first following the midterms, also took aim at the vice president’s statements on Israel, saying he has "great concerns about what I’ve heard coming out of the vice president’s office with regard to Israel."

Asked about Vance's assessment, Pence said, "I disagree with the vice president about the reasons for the midterm election outcome."

"There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said. "As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump."

RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME

But the former vice president emphasized "the reasons for this midterm election were much more complex than gasoline prices or the war in Iran. So, I respectfully disagree with my successor in that regard."

"If the world knows nothing else, the world should know that America stands with Israel. Israel is our most cherished ally. It is the only democracy in the Arab world," Pence a longtime strong supporter of Israel, emphasized.

Pence said he's "very troubled at the way that criticism of Israel on the left and on the right collapses too often into antisemitism and antisemitic rhetoric. There's no place in America for antisemitism on the left or on the right and the people that are wringing their hands about U.S. support for Israel, I get the feeling sometimes they're just using that as a thinly veiled excuse for their antisemitism."

‘HE BLAMED THE JEWS’: GOP CONGRESSMAN LEVELS EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATION AGAINST JD VANCE OVER ELECTION POSTMORTEM

Vance, in an assessment the morning after Election Day, wrote, "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."

The vice president also cited an unnamed pollster in his X post who said voters who had abandoned the GOP wanted the administration to end the conflict, address inflation and the cost of living, put America first and change its relationship with Israel.

A Vance ally, responding to Pence's criticism, told Fox News Digital, "Former Vice President Pence had to retreat into the think tank world because his politics never developed past the Bush-era neocon warmongering that dragged us into the Middle East in the first place. He is laughably out of touch with how people feel in the real world."

VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

Vice President JD Vance points to President Donald Trump at the Republican convention Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

Pence, who served as vice president in Trump's first term, pointed to the president's second term tariffs, the administration's handling of abortion medication and the first family's growing wealth as factors in the GOP's electoral defeat, arguing that Republicans must return to traditional conservative principles to reclaim their congressional majorities.

While the high cost of living and the war in Iran were key issues in the midterms, the Fox News Voter Poll also highlighted that 55% of respondents said government corruption was a "crucial" factor in their vote for Congress, with another 36% saying it was a major factor.

Pence argued that "I don't think you can ignore the air of corruption that's emerged around this administration, the self-dealing. The American people saw a First Family seeing their wealth increase by more than $3 billion including more than a billion dollars in cryptocurrency."

Asked by Fox Digital if he thought the president and his family had improperly profited from being in the White House, Pence answered, "I wouldn't have any way of knowing and wouldn't care to speculate."

"Mike Pence’s total and complete lack of courage caused untold damage to our great country," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle. "If Republican voters cared what Mike Pence had to say, he wouldn’t have had to drop out of the presidential race months before the Iowa caucuses."

The former vice president, referring to the midterm results which saw the Democrats storm back to grab a large House majority, take control of the Senate, and win a majority of the nation's governorships, said it "wasn't just a rout, it was a reckoning."

"I believe our voters rejected President Trump's redirection of our movement toward protectionist tariffs, toward policies of appeasement toward Russia and even Iran, toward marginalizing the right to life, and I think the era of corruption around the Trump administration was very concerning to millions of Americans, including our voters," Pence claimed. "I don't think the American people turned left. I think they were turned off, and that's what explains the outcome of this election."

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Looking forward, Pence said Republicans "now more than ever...need to recommit our party to the conservative principles that have defined our movement for more than 50 years."

"There's no question that the direction the president has taken our party was roundly rejected by the voters," he charged. "The key for success for the party and more importantly, the key for success for the country, is to return the Republican Party to advancing and advocating the conservative principles that have always made America strong and prosperous and free."

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

#6056. Indonesia’s Wiretap Scandal Heralds a Political Showdown

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Southeast Asia Brief: Indonesia’s Wiretap Scandal Heralds a Political Showdown

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia’s former chief of police is arrested on suspicion of wiretapping the president, a Florida cruise ship abandons passengers in Cambodia, and we explore the Southeast Asian dimension of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia’s former chief of police is arrested on suspicion of wiretapping the president, a Florida cruise ship abandons passengers in Cambodia, and we explore the Southeast Asian dimension of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang.

Former police chief charged with spying on president

Shortly after this newsletter was finalized, it was announced vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka had tendered his resignation. The dramatic development comes amidst a growing swell to impeach him, and a dramatic wiretap scandal covered below.

Last Tuesday, Indonesia’s former chief of police and Presidential Chief of Staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo and two other police generals were arrested on suspicion of wiretapping President Prabowo Subianto. That same day, the government flooded Jakarta with more than 20,000 troops.

The development is widely seen as heralding a showdown between the president and his rival-turned-ally, former President Joko Widodo, whose son Gibran Rakabuming Raka serves as vice president.

Since the initial revelations, the story has grown more extraordinary. The presidential palace has accused the men, as well as a fourth police general, of treason, which can carry the death penalty.

The government reportedly suspects them of helping foster protests, which have rocked the government over the past two years.

Police alleged the president was one of some 6,000 people—including top politicians, businesspeople, journalists, and activists—illegally surveilled from 2025 until last month. Prabowo himself apparently suspected that he was being tapped for more than a year.

The political implications are explosive. Listyo is widely seen as Widodo’s man and is part of the “Solo Gang,” a group of officials from Widodo’s hometown of Surakarta, where the former president began his political career as mayor.

Listyo is alleged to have operated as something of a Mr. Fix-It for Widodo in delicate political situations, from intraparty disputes to the 2024 election.

Police investigators have rather pointedly announced that neither Widodo nor his son were on the list of those wiretapped.

The move against Listyo seems to herald a wider move against Widodo, whose political relationship with Prabowo has deteriorated steadily since the 2024 election.

In parliament, there is now a growing push to impeach Gibran. The Supreme Court ruled in October that he had failed to properly prove he had graduated high school, which is a requirement to run for the vice presidency, opening the door for parliament to take action.

Widodo himself is keeping schtum. When asked about the arrest of Listyo and the Supreme Court ruling against Gibran, he has limited his responses to platitudes about respecting the legal process. Gibran has also confined himself to broad statements about respecting legal processes and focusing on his job.

Still, Widodo has also been maneuvering to shore up his position. He has effectively taken over the Indonesian Solidarity Party of which his other son, Kaesang Pangarep, is the general chair. Widodo’s enormous personal popularity gives him some potentially powerful cards to play.

Another impact is that Indonesia is looking at tightening legal controls on wiretapping.

This is not the country’s first wiretapping scandal. In 2022, Reuters revealed that Pegasus spyware, created by Israeli cyber-intelligence firm NSO Group, had been used in Indonesia since 2018 to target politicians and other prominent figures. Evidence later suggested the software was being used by Indonesia’s security services.

Despite the scandal, little action was taken and regulations governing the use of wiretaps remain a mess.

More generally this will only contribute to the sense that the wheels are coming off for Indonesia.

The political elite are gearing up for a round of brutal infighting while Indonesia is facing its worst forest fires in a decade, there is growing pressure on government bonds as the energy shock rockets up the price of fuel subsidies, and the third finance minister in two years takes the helm amid protests from a fed up populace.

Abandon ship. More than 200 passengers were abandoned in Cambodia by a Florida cruise-liner company, Villa Vie Residences, last Wednesday. The ship then steamed toward Singapore with 50 crew aboard and it was later impounded.

The ship, Villa Vie Odyssey, is one of a handful of ships worldwide that offers people the opportunity to reside on it long term. The price of permanent residence ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Rentals started at $3,500 a month.

However, in late October, the company abruptly suspended operations, saying increased fuel costs due to the Iran war had made operations unsustainable. Residents were reportedly given seven hours’ notice.

Problems seem to have been long-running. Passengers recounted two occasions in recent months where the company asked them to pool money to buy fuel for the ship.

And last year—even before the Iran war— Villa Vie Residences was sued for fraud by a plaintiff who had bought a cabin and alleged the company had misrepresented its financial stability.

According to Cambodia’s Ministry of Tourism, there are now 98 passengers left in Cambodia. Others have already left the country.

Growth falters further. Indonesia isn’t the only country where the political elites are playing games while the country struggles.

On Tuesday, the Philippines reported a dismal GDP growth of 2.1 percent. This was below the predicted 3 percent as growth slowed for the fifth consecutive quarter. Inflation also surged to a three-year high of 7.8 percent due to increased fuel prices linked to the Iran war.

Still, the Senate remains absorbed in the impeachment of vice president Sara Duterte. And politicians are pursuing their usual budget shenanigans, unabashed by the enormous scandal that such antics sparked last year.

The Philippines is extremely dependent on fuel imports, and 90 percent of those imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz prior to the Iran war. This means the war has hit hard, with food and fuel inflation eroding consumption. It has had a major impact on the country’s economy as private consumption accounts for roughly three-quarters of the Philippines’ economy.

The other key factors are a 4.8 percent contraction of the agricultural sector and 4 percent contraction in construction. Bad weather hit the former hard, with nearly all senators urging El Niño to be declared a calamity. Meanwhile, the latter has struggled after a massive scandal last year involving the embezzlement of state funds slowed public investment.

Fatal shooting stirs war memories. One civilian was killed and 23 were injured in an Indonesian Army operation in Aceh last Wednesday. Six army personnel were also injured in the incident.

The spark was the raising of a crescent and star flag during a celebration of the prophet Muhammad’s birthday at Pulo Keunari village in the province of Aceh. The flag is associated with Aceh’s former separatist movement.

Despite a 2005 peace agreement, the flag has remained a symbol of ongoing tensions between the province and the central government. In 2013, the provincial government tried to adopt it as Aceh’s official flag but the central government objected.

Accounts of the sequence of events last Wednesday differ. An aide to Aceh’s governor told The Jakarta Post that soldiers had used a loudspeaker to demand the flag be taken down. A soldier then took down the flag, angering the crowd and sparking the clash. The aide added that the resident who died was killed via a gunshot wound to the chest.

Representatives of the military claimed that their attempts to remove the flag were met with stone throwing. The soldiers and accompanying police responded with riot control equipment, including the firing of blank shots and rubber bullets.

In Cambodia, nearly 24,000 foreigners have been deported after scam center raids over the past year; and 15,000 volunteer for military service this year, which is 5,000 more than needed.

Politicians and royals in Malaysia row over a former prime minister’s house arrest.

Rebels cautiously welcome U.S. peace plans for Myanmar; the Economist reported how rebels’ Starlink terminals are being unpredictably turned off; and Myanmar migrants reject the government’s new IDs.

Philippines police find child abuse material on devices owned by Meghan Markle’s dad.

China buys influence in Thailand media; opposition leaders allege they had their phones hacked ahead of a no confidence vote; a former Miss Thailand is accused of stealing millions from a charity; two Uyghurs face deportation to China; and a book about Thailand’s king is banned on national security grounds.

Vietnam security services may have abducted an Australian and a Norwegian activist in Cambodia; and To Lam visits Japan.

In Focus: Nvidia Scandal’s Southeast Asian Background

The affair between Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, is making headlines worldwide, with the scandal containing an almost filmic mix of geopolitical implications and salacity.

One aspect that bears further scrutiny is the Southeast Asian aspect. Alice Huang was a senior executive, and self-described CEO, of Megaspeed, a company based in Singapore with offices in Malaysia and Indonesia.

The company has been under scrutiny by the U.S. government since 2024 over its alleged sanctions-busting activity smuggling top-end Nvidia chips into China. Singapore also conducted its own investigation and detained Alice Huang in 2025.

The scandal reflects that Singapore, and Southeast Asia more generally, has become a hub for China’s chip sanction-busting efforts on a massive scale. Some smuggle them into China. Other companies operate in a gray zone, building data centers with top-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia and then leasing their processing power to China.

Culper Research, a short seller that flagged Jensen Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang back in May, estimated that 20 percent of Nvidia’s compute revenues were driven by China “via illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.” (You can read more on this topic in FP’s China Brief.)

The latest scandal comes against the background of numerous others. In 2025, the United States launched another investigation into whether DeepSeek had used Nvidia chips smuggled via Singapore.

In May, Taiwan arrested three people suspected of planning to smuggle Nvidia chips into China via an unnamed Southeast Asian country.

In late October, Malaysia estimated that a single syndicate was behind at least five cases where Malaysia authorities had seized smuggled ⁠chips that were cumulatively ​worth more than 100 million ringgit ($24.6 million).

These murky happenings reflect that the region is deeply enmeshed with both China and the United States’ economies and has its own thriving tech ecosystem.

Malaysia has become a thriving data center hub, welcoming investment from both superpowers. The country of 34.4 million people now has half as much artificial intelligence compute power as the entire European Union.

But, for those in the region who have tried to not let geopolitics affect business, or at least turn tensions to their advantage, the walls may be closing in.

Busts in Malaysia reflect ongoing U.S. pressure to crack down. And, on Friday, Bloomberg reported Nvidia was stepping up its tracking of chips in Southeast Asia to crack down on smuggling.

Pressure is also coming from Taiwan. It recently canceled trade talks with Malaysia, which could threaten future investment in the latter’s thriving semiconductor space, due to anger over comments in which Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim appeared to accept China’s right to use force to assimilate Taiwan.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph

#6055. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department’s Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6054. Another Trump heavyweight revealed to be living on military base as Cabinet roster grows

Former CIA station chief Dan Hoffman examines reported Iranian threats that prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his family to relocate to a military base. He also discusses allegations of Iranian cyberattacks in France and reported cooperation between Iran and Russia to circumvent U.S. military and economic restrictions.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has been living at a military installation in the Washington, D.C., area for months, joining a growing roster of senior Trump administration officials residing in military housing, three sources familiar with the arrangement confirmed to Fox News Digital.

A source familiar with the arrangement did not elaborate on the reason for the move earlier this year. Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Justice for comment.

Among the other top officials residing on military installations is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who recently relocated amid reported threats linked to Iran.

The living arrangements have placed senior civilian officials in housing traditionally associated with military leadership, amid security concerns ranging from reported threats tied to drug cartels to fears of Iranian retaliation.

US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice on April 7, 2026. (Getty Images)

Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, also quietly relocated from her Washington apartment to military housing after law enforcement flagged threats tied to drug cartels, The New York Times reported in March. The Times also cited threats related to backlash over her handling of the Epstein files, although the Justice Department disputed that explanation.

Iran has intensified efforts to target Americans, including current and former U.S. officials, as Bessent recently relocated to a military base amid threats linked to Tehran, a source familiar with the situation confirmed to Fox News Digital Wednesday.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase, which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a different source familiar with the move told Fox News Digital Wednesday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.

SECRET SERVICE CHIEF SAYS THREATS AGAINST PROTECTEES UP 40%, CITES INTERNET AND MENTAL HEALTH

War Secretary Pete Hegseth, far left, and Vice President JD Vance, far right, laugh together during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House, April 28, 2026. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders.

ARMY SECRETARY DAN DRISCOLL SUBMITS RESIGNATION TO TRUMP

President Donald Trump attends a Cabinet meeting at the White House in Washington on May 27, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation.

The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base.

Other officials previously reported to have used military housing include former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll. The arrangements have involved different installations.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.
